docs.title: Z-Vision Generator
docs.text:
Local AI image and video generation — hassle-free and fun. No tangled node graphs, no cloud dependencies, just prompts and results. Runs on macOS (Apple Silicon / MLX) and on Windows and Linux with NVIDIA CUDA through diffusers.

Z-Vision Generator gives you a unified CLI for both image and video generation, with batch runs, prompt variables, LoRA support, upscaling, and more — all while abstracting away platform-specific details.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Image generation — text-to-image with Z-Image, FLUX.2 Klein (4B/9B) and Krea 2 Turbo model families, plus Ideogram 4 (FP8 on macOS/MLX, NF4 on Windows and Linux)
  • Video generation — text-to-video and image-to-video with platform-specific LTX aliases, audio included by default
  • Cross-platform — automatic backend selection: MLX on macOS, diffusers/CUDA on Windows and Linux for images, and the shared diffusers/CUDA LTX backend on Windows and Linux for video
  • Prompt system — YAML prompt files with variables ({red|blue|green}), structured prompts, snippets, and batch runs
  • Model store — central ~/.ziv/ directory with bare-name resolution, aliases, local paths, and supported HuggingFace model references
  • LoRA support — single or stacked, configurable weights, bare-name resolution (image and video)
  • Image upscale — generate small → Lanczos → img2img refine → CAS sharpen
  • Video upscale — --upscale 2 renders at half size, upsamples the latents 2× and refines at full size, so the clip keeps the requested size, on macOS and on Windows/Linux
  • Reference images — img2img steering from any starting image
  • Model variants — image quantization across supported image backends, plus macOS MLX video Q4/Q8 aliases
  • Post-processing — contrast, saturation, and CAS sharpening (image only)
  • Interactive controls — skip, quit, pause, and repeat during image batch runs; Web UI video jobs can be cancelled
  • Live preview — the Web UI shows the image taking shape at 25/50/75% of the steps so you can skip early (preview only, never saved). Supported for Z-Image, FLUX.2 Klein, Krea 2 and Ideogram 4 on every platform

docs.title: Testing Conventions
docs.text:
• Tests live in tests/. Name files test_<module>.py, functions test_<behavior>.
  • Group related tests in Test-prefixed classes.
  • Never import or instantiate real backends/models. Use unittest.mock.MagicMock with controlled return values.
  • Mock backend pattern: a MagicMock with .text_to_image.return_value = Image.new("RGB", (64, 64)) (see _make_mock_backend() in tests/test_workflow.py).
  • Use conftest.py::_make_args(**overrides) to build minimal argparse.Namespace objects.
  • Use tmp_path fixture for filesystem operations.
  • Use @pytest.mark.parametrize for data-driven tests with many input/output pairs.
  • Tests that run the real ffmpeg and ffprobe (in tests/test_video_probe.py, tests/test_video_splice.py and tests/test_video_tail.py) are marked to skip when the tools are missing and are meant to be run locally with ffmpeg installed; run them before changing the extend join. Everything else mocks ffmpeg.
  • Skip heavy dependencies: pytest.importorskip("torch"), @pytest.mark.skipif(sys.platform == ...) for platform-specific tests.
  • Assert behavior and machine-readable contracts, not documentation prose, help text wording, CSS utility classes, source-code text, or incidental selector details.
  • String assertions are appropriate only when the string is the contract under test, such as routes, config keys, storage keys, parser options, event names, filenames, enum values, structured statuses, and accessibility or control names required for operability.

docs.title: Code Style
docs.text:
• Python 3.14+, from __future__ import annotations in every .py file.
  • Modern type syntax: str | None, list[str], dict[str, Any]. Never use Optional, Union, List, Dict, or Tuple from typing.
  • Import order: stdlib → third-party → local (zvisiongenerator.*). Separate each group with a blank line.
  • Use TYPE_CHECKING guards for imports that pull in heavy runtime dependencies (torch, mflux, diffusers).
  • Line length limit: 200 (enforced by ruff).
  • Docstrings: Google-style. Module-level docstrings on all non-trivial modules. First line is an imperative fragment. Multi-line use Args:, Returns:, Raises: sections.

docs.title: Backend Protocol
docs.text:
Platform backends live in backends/mac/image.py (mflux/MLX), backends/cuda/image/backend.py (Windows/Linux diffusers image), backends/mac/video.py (MLX video), and backends/cuda/video/backend.py (Windows/Linux diffusers video). Image backends implement the ImageBackend Protocol from core/image_backend.py; video backends implement the VideoBackend Protocol from core/video_backend.py. The prompt-enhancer LLM follows the same split: backends/mac/prompt_enhancer.py (mlx-lm) and backends/cuda/prompt_enhancer.py (transformers) implement the PromptEnhancer Protocol from core/prompt_enhancer.py. Backend and accelerator selection stays centralized in backends/__init__.py — never branch on sys.platform elsewhere to pick a backend. OS-level checks unrelated to backends (drive listings, ffmpeg install hints, terminal handling) are fine where they are needed.

SeedVR2, the plain upscale of existing images, is macOS-only and has its own small Protocol, SeedVR2Upscaler in core/seedvr2.py, implemented by backends/mac/seedvr2.py (mflux). supports_seedvr2() and get_seedvr2_upscaler() in backends/__init__.py expose it, so other code asks for the capability instead of checking the platform. seedvr2_loader.py loads it through a stored 8-bit copy in the same way image_model_loader.py does for image models, and tests/test_mflux_seedvr2_contract.py records the mflux surface it relies on; re-run it on every mflux bump.

Backends are grouped by platform: backends/cuda/ (Windows and Linux) and backends/mac/. A task with helpers of its own gets a folder (cuda/image/, cuda/video/); what two tasks share stays one level up. The platform folders never import from each other. Platform selection still happens only in backends/__init__.py.

Windows and Linux video resolution is config-driven through video_model_presets.ltx.diffusers: ltx-4 and ltx-8 both resolve to default_repo, quantize maps each name to its level (there is no unquantized path), and utils.config.ltx_load_options turns the config into the backend's load arguments for both the CLI and the Web UI. Only distilled LTX-2.3 checkpoints are supported.

cuda/video/backend.load_model keeps LTX within the system memory of a 32 GB machine and the GPU memory of a 10 GB one. The rules a change must keep:

  • The text encoder and the transformer never share system memory unless both fit (_check_system_memory). When they do not, they take turns: the transformer is released while the text encoder encodes each new prompt (_encode_prompt, _attach_transformer, _release_transformer); when they do, the text encoder stays loaded between prompts. LoRAs are applied when the transformer is attached.
  • The transformer is the single-file checkpoint in video_model_presets.ltx.diffusers.transformer. cuda/video/weights prepares it and the text encoder once per level under <models>/<alias>@q<bits>/, streaming tensor by tensor through safetensors_stream so a 46 GB file never sits in memory.
  • In low-memory mode the transformer streams to the GPU block by block (block_streaming): FP8 with diffusers' group offloading, NF4 with stream_blocks, because group offloading leaves bitsandbytes' quantization state on the CPU. The VAEs and vocoder move to the GPU only to encode or decode. Video never uses enable_model_cpu_offload().
  • Nothing may hold a full-length activation per token beyond the hidden states: the token-wise layers run in chunks (token_chunking), image-to-video's per-token timesteps are applied per run of equal timesteps (timestep_runs), and the final pass returns latents that streaming_decode decodes a few frames at a time. Each keeps diffusers' output unchanged, and its tests compare against diffusers.
  • Clips are written by video_encode (H.264 CRF 18 and AAC, as on macOS).

backends/cuda/video/backend.py passes the distilled sigma tables from diffusers.pipelines.ltx2.utils on every generation call, with num_inference_steps equal to their length and every guidance term at its neutral value (_DISTILLED_GUIDANCE); diffusers' own defaults for the audio, spatio-temporal and modality terms over-cook a distilled model. Fewer steps than the table keep its first sigma and its tail. The --upscale 2 flow is two-stage:

  1. Stage 1 runs the generation pipeline at half the requested size with output_type="latent".
  2. An LTX2LatentUpsamplePipeline upsamples the latents 2×. It is built around the generation pipeline's own VAE and is never moved with .to() or given CPU offload, since either would re-hook that shared VAE. In low-memory mode the upsampler model waits on the CPU and visits the GPU only for this pass.
  3. Stage 2 calls the same LoRA-bearing generation pipeline at full size with the upsampled latents, the stage-1 audio latents and the stage-2 sigmas. The scheduler is swapped for a static-shift copy for that call only and restored afterwards, even when the call fails.

The upsampler weights are one safetensors file resolved with hf_hub_download from video_model_presets.ltx.diffusers.latent_upsampler (repo, filename; read with utils.config.ltx_latent_upsampler_source) before the generation pipeline loads, and only when upscaling. Both stages report steps as one run under the video_upscale_stage_1 and video_upscale_stage_2 phases, as the macOS backend does.

Extending a clip is an optional capability, not part of VideoBackend: the VideoExtender Protocol in core/video_backend.py declares extend_video(model, source, prompt, *, extend_frames, seed, steps, segment_dir, audio_output, step_callback=None), which both LTX backends implement. Callers gate on supports_video_extend() in backends/__init__.py (beside supports_video_audio()) and look the method up on the backend; the Web UI contract drops the extend workflow, and the CLI refuses --extend, when it is false.

On Windows and Linux, load_model(mode="extend") loads LTX2ConditionPipeline, and extend_video pins the tail frames with LTX2VideoCondition(frames=tail, index=0, strength=1.0) in a one-stage window at the source's size and frame rate. diffusers gives every audio token one timestep, so cuda/video/audio_carry pins the carried sound itself, as the macOS denoise mask does: the tail's sound (read by utils/video_tail.read_source_tail_audio at the audio VAE's rate) becomes a log-mel spectrogram with the LTX audio processor's settings and is encoded with audio_vae.encode(...)[0].mode(); pin_audio_prefix is a transformer pre-hook that, on every forward pass, puts those tokens (packed and normalized with the pipeline's _pack_audio_latents and _normalize_audio_latents) clean at the start of audio_hidden_states and gives them audio_timestep 0, leaving audio_sigma per sample; restore_audio_prefix puts the clean latent back into the result's audio latents (output_type="latent" returns them denormalized as (batch, 8, tokens, 16)) before they are decoded. The window's frames go to the segment through utils/video_splice.write_segment_frames. tests/test_diffusers_ltx2_contract.py pins the diffusers names and layouts this uses.

The Windows/Linux video backend is CUDA-only. Validation happens lazily during backend load so importing the package or running non-video code paths does not require torch, diffusers, or a GPU.

The Windows/Linux diffusers image backend is also CUDA-only. Validation happens lazily during image backend load so importing the package or running non-image code paths does not require torch, diffusers, or a GPU.

docs.title: Workflow Stages
docs.text: Image stage functions in workflows/image_stages.py have the uniform signature (ImageGenerationRequest, ImageWorkingArtifacts) -> StageOutcome. Video stage functions in workflows/video_stages.py have the signature (VideoGenerationRequest, VideoWorkingArtifacts) -> StageOutcome. Stages are composed dynamically by build_workflow() and build_video_workflow(). A video workflow starts with resolve_prompt_stage, which composes the scene and the prompt into the text the model receives (compose_video_prompt), and enhance_prompt_stage applies a planned scene and action rewrite. A job whose arguments carry an extend_source swaps the generation stage for the extend pair: extend_video (calls extend_video on the backend for the new segment only) and join_clips (utils/video_splice.splice_clips joins the segment onto the untouched source and removes the temporary segment directory). The extend variant has no strip_audio stage, since the joined clip already has the right audio; its provenance workflow is extend, with source_video and extend_frames recorded. build_upscale_workflow() upscales an existing image (load_source_stage → upscale_stage → sharpen_stage → save_image_stage); the Web UI runs it through WebRunner.submit_upscale_job and upscale_runner.run_upscale, which emits the same events as a one-image batch, without preflight or the batch loop. build_seedvr2_upscale_workflow() is the plain upscale (resolve_prompt_stage → load_source_stage → seedvr2_stages.upscale_stage → save_image_stage), chosen when the request's upscale_method is seedvr2; it does not sharpen. The tier is chosen by utils/seedvr2.pick_seedvr2_tier from the seedvr2 config block and the Mac's memory budget, and generation.upscale.method records seedvr2 or creative in the saved file.

docs.title: Review Before Upscaling
docs.text: --review pauses a generation after the small render of an upscale until the user approves or discards it. The review state lives in SkipSignal (utils/interactive.py), the shared wait in review.py, and images pass through review_stage before upscale_stage. Video passes a review keyword to the backend: only the macOS backend (mac/video) honours it, the CUDA one (cuda/video/backend) refuses, and supports_video_upscale_review() in backends/__init__.py tells the form, server and CLI whether to offer it. The Web UI sends approve and discard through the job controls and shows a video review from GET /jobs/{id}/review. Everything stays in memory while the review waits, so an approved output equals one made without review.

docs.title: Job Phases: Preflight and Generation
docs.text:
Every image and video job (CLI and Web UI) runs in two phases, and only one model is resident at a time:

  1. Preflight (preflight.run_preflight) runs before the generation model loads. It plans every iteration with plan_iterations (seed, {a|b} expansion, enhancement settings) and, when any iteration asks for auto enhancement, loads the prompt enhancer, rewrites those prompts, closes the enhancer and frees accelerator memory. It returns a frozen JobPlan (core/job_plan.py).
  2. Generation: the entry point loads the model and passes the plan to run_batch / run_video_batch as the required plan= argument. Runners raise ValueError for a cancelled plan or one whose length differs from the batch, and RuntimeError when an iteration is out of order. Retry and repeat keep the planned text and draw a new random seed.

JobPlan.iterations holds one IterationPlan per iteration in run → set → prompt order, the order the runners loop in. Each carries seed, resolved_prompt, enhanced_prompt and enhance_status (off, enhanced, failed, skipped); video iterations also carry scene, resolved_scene and enhanced_scene, and a video rewrite returns the scene and the action together. EnhanceSettings.parts (both, action or None for auto) picks what a video rewrite writes; resolve_parts() turns it into action or both per job (auto means action when extending a clip that has a scene, and a blank scene always means both). A rewrite that keeps the scene returns EnhancePairResult.scene == "", so enhanced_scene is None, no enhanced_scene is stored in the metadata, and the provenance scene is the user's own, with scene_input repeating it. The workflow's enhance_prompt_stage only applies the planned rewrite; no workflow stage calls the LLM.

Entry points own the control signal. image_cli.main creates the SkipSignal and its key listener before preflight and stops it after run_batch; Web UI image and video jobs pass their control signal to both phases. Video jobs offer only Quit: run_video_batch checks it before each video and raises from the step callback so a running video stops at its next denoising step, then emits batch_cancelled. During preflight there is a control boundary before each rewrite and a final one after the enhancer is released: skip skips the next rewrite, pause waits, quit cancels, and repeat is dropped. A rewrite stopped by the user (the cancelled callback saw Next or Quit) is skipped, never failed. On Quit, preflight releases the enhancer and memory before emitting batch_cancelled.

Preflight events (none carry eta_secs, avg_secs or elapsed_secs):

Event When Payload preflight_started first event of every preflight mode, total_iterations, total_rewrites enhancer_loading 0..n, only when the enhancer loads; cpu when it runs on the CPU mode, phase prompts_enhancing once per rewrite, after its boundary mode, index, total prompt_enhance_failed a rewrite failed without a user stop mode, index, total, message job_paused / job_resumed pause at a boundary mode, completed_iterations, total_iterations batch_cancelled Quit (web: job_cancelled) mode, completed_iterations, total_iterations preflight_finished last event unless cancelled mode, total_iterations, enhanced, failed, skipped

prompt_started also carries the iteration's enhance_status.

Tests must never run the real memory cleanup: patch zvisiongenerator.preflight.release_accelerator_memory (and zvisiongenerator.web.web_runner.release_accelerator_memory for web jobs), or pass release_memory= to run_preflight.

To add pre-load work (for example LoRA validation or a memory-fit check), add a field to JobPlan or IterationPlan and a private step in run_preflight. There is no stage pipeline or registry; promote preflight.py to a package only once it holds several concerns.

docs.title: Web Job Queue
docs.text:
WebRunner (web/web_runner.py) runs every Web UI job on a single worker thread. Generation jobs are never refused for being second: _submit_job registers the job, publishes job_submitted, appends it to the FIFO queue and dispatches it, all under _jobs_lock, so the worker receives jobs in queue order. When the worker reaches a job, _claim takes it off the queue and publishes job_started (status running, started_at; elapsed_secs counts from here). A job removed with cancel_queued, clear_queue or shutdown is no longer queued, so the claim skips it even if its work item was already picked up; it ends with job_cancelled and reason: "removed".

The active job is the claimed one or, between jobs, the head of the queue; every other unfinished generation job is queued, with a 1-based queue_position. GET /api/jobs and /api/workspace return them as active_job and queued_jobs, and a job is never in both. DELETE /api/jobs/queue removes the queued jobs and keeps the active one. Actions that need the model memory to themselves (manual prompt enhancement, saving a quantized copy, deleting models or LoRAs) still wait until no generation job is running or queued.

docs.title: Data Types
docs.text: Use @dataclass(frozen=True) for immutable value objects (inputs, detection results). Use mutable @dataclass only for working state. No pydantic or attrs.

docs.title: Config Layering
docs.text: CLI flags > model preset variant > model preset family > global defaults. Config is a plain dict loaded from YAML, not a dataclass.

docs.title: Web Model Inventory
docs.text:
A repo-id alias can declare its image family in config via model_alias_families (for example ideo: ideogram4). The Web UI inventory and workspace bootstrap consult this declared family as an offline fast-path, so a known alias is surfaced without the network detect_image_model round-trip that a bare Hugging Face repo id would otherwise require. Content-based detection for arbitrary local model directories is unaffected; only aliases with a declared family skip detection.

Per-model Web UI capability flags — supports_img2img, supports_upscale, supports_scheduler, supports_json_prompt, supports_first_sigma, dimension_min, dimension_max, and dimension_step — are data-driven: they originate in the model_presets family entries, flow through resolve_defaults, and are emitted into the SPA's ImageModelDefaults. Families that do not set them inherit permissive defaults (img2img, upscale and scheduler enabled, JSON caption and first-sigma disabled, 16/null/16 dimension bounds), so gating is centralized in config rather than branching on family in the web layer.

docs.title: Error Conventions
docs.text: Raise ValueError, FileNotFoundError, RuntimeError directly with descriptive f-string messages. Use warnings.warn() with stacklevel=2 for non-fatal conditions. Add a custom exception class only when callers must catch it distinctly (for example JobConflictError in web/web_runner.py) or as a private sentinel.

docs.title: Web UI Confirmations
docs.text:
Ask the user to approve an action with ConfirmDialog (frontend/src/lib/components/molecules/), never window.confirm. It has no title: it shows the question, an optional line of information, and a cancel button plus a confirm button named after the action (danger-styled for destructive actions). Enter confirms (except on the focused cancel button), Esc cancels, and a held key never confirms; while it is open, no other key reaches the page or a viewer underneath. Call requestConfirm({ question, info, confirmLabel }), which resolves true on confirm, or render <ConfirmDialog> directly when the dialog needs a body or stays open while the action runs (pending).

Let the user choose a path on the server's machine with PathField, or PathInput (a path box with completion) and PathBrowser (the browse dialog) where a field needs its own layout. Each takes a browse purpose; the purposes, with their folder or file kind and accepted extensions, live in web/path_browser.py, so add one there for a new kind of path.

docs.title: Web UI Toasts
docs.text:
Report the outcome of an action with addToast(message, type, options) from $lib/state/toasts.svelte. One toast shows at a time at the bottom centre of the page content (pages with a fixed left sidebar set --toast-inset-left); the rest wait their turn, shown as "+N". A repeat of a waiting or showing message merges into it ("×2"), and an error goes ahead of every non-error. Each tone has a default time on screen (success 2.5 s, info 4 s, warning 7 s); errors stay until dismissed, or give way after 8 s once other toasts are waiting, and hovering or focusing a toast pauses it. Pass { action: { label, run } } for one follow-up such as Retry, and { timeout } only when the default doesn't fit. An action that acts on a page must not outlive it: keep the id addToast returns and call dismissToast(id) in the page's onDestroy. Raise one toast per action, and skip it when the screen already shows the result.

Send requests through api in $lib/api/client, which throws ApiError with the HTTP status and the server's detail. Show a failed request with errorText(err, fallback), never err.message, which holds the method, path and raw body. Offer Retry only when isRetryable(err): a 4xx means the server refused the input, and the same request fails the same way again.

docs.title: Web UI Design System
docs.text:
The Web UI has one design system. Its tokens live in @theme in frontend/src/app/global.css, and its component classes are the ui-* classes in the same file. Build pages from the shared components in frontend/src/lib/components/ (Button, Input, Select, Toggle, Badge, Panel, Segmented, ActionBar, PageHeader, KeyValueList, Alert, EmptyState, InspectorSection, InspectorRow) or, where no component fits, the ui-* classes (for example ui-chip), rather than styling elements by hand.

  • Size: controls are 28px (h-control), small ones 22px, rows 30px. Buttons that sit together share one height; inside an ActionBar every button is 36px and the one marked main takes the remaining width.
  • Type: four sizes only: text-meta (11px), text-ui (12px), text-content (13px), text-title (16px). Nunito (font-heading) is for titles, area names and the main action; monospace is for numbers, paths and shortcuts.
  • Labels: field and row labels are sentence case (ui-label). The one small-caps style (ui-area-label) names areas: panels, sections, table headers and menu groups.
  • Shape and surfaces: corners are 4px for chips and badges, 6px for controls and 10px for containers. Overlays (menus, popovers, tooltips, toasts, dialogs) use bg-overlay, darker than any page surface, with a faint ring and never a drop shadow; bg-raised is for section header bands and bg-fill for the prompt box.
  • No borders: containers are separated by shade, and buttons, fields, chips and badges are filled shapes. Dividers between rows and sections stay. Draw an outline only where it means something: focus, a field with an error, the selected tile, and the dashed edge of drop zones and add buttons. Segmented controls are a recessed well with the chosen option as a lighter pill.
  • Main action: each section (a bar, panel, form, dialog or popover) has at most one main action, a primary button: teal fill and a bold Nunito label. Every other button in the section is secondary.
  • Reference pages: Config and Models centre their content at max-w-page (1200px), with the page bar lined up to it. Settings use label-left rows (FormField layout="row"), and tables use ui-table-comfortable.
  • Colour: neutrals are Graphite greys with no tint. Teal means on, selected or the main action; coral (accent-coral, Blob's beret) marks $snippets and amber {a|b} choices; red is for errors and destructive actions, which always show red text. Info messages stay teal, never coral. Text is at least 4.5:1 on every surface. Use tokens, never raw palette classes or colour literals; make check fails on them.
  • Focus: every control shows the same 2px teal outline with a 2px offset.

docs.title: Test Strategy
docs.text: Mock heavy image and video dependencies in tests. Diffusers backend tests patch the lazy runtime loader, torch CUDA checks, upsampler weight download and loading, export helpers, and PIL image loading so the suite never instantiates a real model, downloads weights, or requires a real CUDA device. Platform dispatch, alias resolution, and Web inventory tests should assert behavior through config and protocol boundaries rather than backend internals.

docs.title: Vendored LTX
docs.text:
packages/ltx_core_mlx and packages/ltx_pipelines_mlx are vendored from dgrauet/ltx-2-mlx. They are not published to PyPI, and PyPI rejects direct-URL dependencies, so they live in the repository. Never edit them by hand.

  • Pin. LTX_COMMIT in the Makefile must be the commit of a release tag; the comment above it names the tag.
  • Update. make update-ltx replaces both packages with the pinned commit. It does not carry their dependencies: mirror the dependencies of upstream's packages/*/pyproject.toml into ours by hand, macOS-only and capped at the minor version that upstream's uv.lock tests (for example mlx-arsenal>=0.2.4,<0.3).
  • Internals we rely on. backends/mac/video.py uses upstream attributes and call shapes that are not public API. Re-check each on every bump. tests/test_ltx_mlx_contract.py pins their names and signatures by introspection, and the mocked tests in tests/test_video_upscale.py cover our calls:
    • _pending_loras on the pipeline (LoRAs applied at load)
    • the duck-typed stepwise slot and its bind(..., stage=) contract, which returns the stage's on_step callable
    • _pre_denoise_flush(video_state, audio_state) (guards against the Metal watchdog) and _decode_and_save_video(frame_rate=, seed=)
    • dit, load(), prompt_encoder, video_patchifier, audio_patchifier, low_memory, and image_conditioner (__call__(fn, free_after=) and resolve_crf)
    • resetting vae_decoder, audio_decoder and vocoder to None to free the decoders
    • utils._orchestration.combined_image_conditionings, utils.args.ImageConditioningInput, and utils.helpers.create_noised_state(legacy_scalar_blend=True)
    • ltx_core_mlx's X0Model, snap_output_dimensions(two_stage=), compute_video_latent_shape, compute_audio_token_count, compute_audio_positions, compute_video_positions and aggressive_cleanup
    • scheduler.shorten_schedule, DISTILLED_SIGMAS and STAGE_2_SIGMAS, and utils.samplers.denoise_loop with its on_step(step_idx, total, video_x0, sigma) signature
    • for review before upscaling: _stage1 (shadowed per call), Stage1Result.video_tokens/audio_tokens/latent_dims, _load_decoders, dit/_loaded (restored after the preview decode), and the model state released after an aborted generation
    • DistilledPipeline.generate_and_save for upscale, and BasePipeline's gemma_model_id default, the transformer-file preference order and the low_memory and low_ram_streaming constructor arguments
    • Extending a clip (LtxVideoBackend.extend_video), video side: conditioning.types.VideoConditionByLatentIndex(frame_indices, clean_latent, strength) pins the carried tail at the start of the window; retake.encode_video_tensor(encoder, video_tensor) and utils.media_io.video_preprocess(frames, height, width) encode the tail frames inside image_conditioner(fn, free_after=)
    • Extending a clip, audio side: ltx_core_mlx.utils.audio.load_audio(path, target_sample_rate, start_time, max_duration, mono) reads the tail's sound at its position in the file; audio_vae.encode_audio(waveform, sample_rate, encoder, processor) encodes it inside audio_conditioner(fn, free_after=); extend_distilled.fit_audio_latent(audio_latent, audio_tokens) fits the (1, 8, T, 16) latent before audio_patchifier.patchify, and extend_distilled.carry_audio_tokens(frame_rate, carry_pixel_frames) gives the token count
    • Extending a clip, decode: the pipeline's _loaded flag (cleared with dit = None so the next load() reloads the transformer), video_decoder_block.load() and video_decoder_block.video_decoder (the diffusion decoder is rejected), video_vae.VideoDecoder.tiled_decode(latent, tiling_config), video_vae._compute_decode_tiling(latent_shape, frame_rate, budget_bytes) (which may return None or temporal tiles), video_vae.decode_cache_limit(), video_vae.stream_chunks_to_ffmpeg(chunks, proc) and video_vae._ffmpeg_sink(cmd), and audio_decoder_block.__call__(audio_latent)
    • Extending a clip: ltx_core_mlx.utils.audio.load_audio returns an AudioData whose .waveform and .sample_rate are passed to encode_audio, and video_patchifier.patchify and audio_patchifier.patchify return (tokens, dims) tuples, so the tokens are patchify(...)[0]
  • Cache limit. low_ram_streaming makes the pipeline set the MLX buffer-cache limit to 0 for the whole process. backends/mac/memory.mlx_cache_limit scopes that to model construction and each generation, then restores the previous limit.

docs.title: Releasing
docs.text:
Pushing a v* tag runs the Release workflow, which builds the package, publishes it to PyPI and creates a GitHub Release. The package version comes from the tag (hatch-vcs), so the tag must be a valid PEP 440 version:

  • Final releases: vX.Y.Z, e.g. v0.13.0.
  • Betas: vX.Y.ZbN, e.g. v0.13.0b1, then b2, b3, … before the final vX.Y.Z. Use aN and rcN the same way for alphas and release candidates.

Pre-release tags are published as GitHub pre-releases, and pip installs them only with --pre or an exact pin (pip install z-vision-generator==0.13.0b1). Before tagging, move the [Unreleased] CHANGELOG entries under a ## [<version>] - <date> heading in a chore(release): v<version> commit whose body lists the release highlights. PyPI never accepts the same version twice, so a broken release needs a new tag.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Python 3.14+
  • uv package manager (required — pip is not supported)
  • macOS: Apple Silicon (M1+) — mflux requires MLX
  • Windows: NVIDIA GPU, RTX 20-series (Turing) or newer including RTX 50-series, with NVIDIA driver 580 or newer
  • Linux: NVIDIA GPU, RTX 20-series (Turing) or newer including RTX 50-series, with NVIDIA driver 580 or newer
  • Video: ffmpeg

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
# Install globally — provides `ziv`, `ziv-ui`, `ziv-image`, `ziv-video`, and `ziv-model`
uv tool install z-vision-generator

# Install globally from repository
uv tool install -e git+https://github.com/knuthelge/ZVisionGenerator.git

# Or, for development
git clone https://github.com/knuthelge/ZVisionGenerator && cd ZVisionGenerator
uv sync

uv is required. This package cannot be installed with pip — some dependencies require uv-specific resolution that pip does not support.

Note: Video generation requires ffmpeg. On Windows and Linux, image and video generation use diffusers/CUDA and fail fast when PyTorch cannot see an NVIDIA CUDA device. If the error mentions the driver, update the NVIDIA driver to 580 or newer.

docs.title: Image Generation
docs.text:
# Local model (bare name resolved from ~/.ziv/models/)
ziv-image -m my-model --prompt "a beautiful sunset"

# HuggingFace model (downloaded automatically)
ziv-image -m Tongyi-MAI/Z-Image-Turbo --prompt "a cat"

# From a prompts file with multiple runs
ziv-image -m my-model -p prompts.yaml -r 3

docs.title: Video Generation
docs.text:
Use MODEL below as ltx-4 or ltx-8 (4-bit or 8-bit) on every platform.

# Text-to-video with LTX (4-bit)
ziv-video -m ltx-4 --prompt "A cat walking through a garden"

# Image-to-video with your platform alias
ziv-video -m MODEL --image photo.jpg --prompt "Camera slowly zooms in"

# Batch from prompts file with your platform alias
ziv-video -m MODEL -p prompts.yaml -r 3

docs.title: Choosing a Video Model
docs.text: ltx-4 needs the least memory; ltx-8 is closer to the full model. On Windows and Linux, ltx-4 needs about 20 GB of system memory and ltx-8 about 27 GB, and the first run of each takes a while to download and prepare the model. See the Video Guide.

docs.title: Model & LoRA Management
docs.text:
# Convert a Z-Image checkpoint
ziv-model model -i checkpoint.safetensors --name my-model

# Import a local LoRA
ziv-model lora -i /path/to/style.safetensors --name my-style

# List installed assets
ziv-model list

docs.title: Web UI
docs.text:
# Start the Web UI
ziv ui

# From a repository checkout
uv run ziv ui --no-browser

# Keep it running after you close the terminal, then stop it later
ziv ui --background
ziv ui --background-stop

By default, the Web UI listens on http://127.0.0.1:8080/ and opens your browser automatically. If port 8080 is busy, Z-Vision Generator chooses the next available local port and prints the final address in the terminal. If a local environment is missing required Web UI packages, ziv ui and ziv-ui print repair guidance for the base install instead of failing with an import traceback.

ziv ui --background starts the Web UI, prints its address and gives you the prompt back; the server keeps running after you close the terminal. ziv ui --background-stop stops every running Web UI, including ones running in the foreground in another terminal, and any job they are running.

While a generation is running, the Web UI keeps the active job attached to the current browser tab. Refreshing the tab reconnects to the running job when the server still has it, and stale completed or missing jobs are cleared automatically. Job controls are shown only when the running job supports them.

You can keep working while a job runs: change the settings and press Add to queue (the Generate button while jobs are active, or ⌘/Ctrl+↵). Queued jobs run one after another, in order, and use the settings they had when you added them. They are listed under the job card as Up next, where each one can be removed or its settings copied back into the form with Load settings; Clear queue removes them all (after asking) and never stops the running job. If a job fails, the next one starts anyway. The queue is shared by every open tab and is kept in the server's memory, so stopping the server clears it. While jobs are running or queued, the manual Enhance prompt button is unavailable, because the enhancer would need the same memory; auto enhancement still runs inside each job.

The Prompts page builds prompt files visually: snippets, sets of prompts, and per-prompt enhancement. See Prompt Builder.

Workspace settings are remembered in the browser between visits and restarts, as long as the Web UI starts on the same port. Choosing a different model applies that model's defaults. LoRAs are remembered per model family: switching to a model of another family brings back the LoRAs you last used with that family (or none), and switching between models of the same family keeps them. Reuse settings, Load settings on a queued job and Extend use exactly the LoRAs the source was made with, so a source made without LoRAs clears them.

If the server can't start a job with the current settings, for example image-to-image without a reference image, the reason shows above the Generate button and in a notice. It goes away when you change a setting.

To run the same job from a terminal, press the terminal button in the Settings header. It copies a ziv image or ziv video command with the current model, prompt, LoRAs and settings, writing to the Web UI's output folder. The CLI has no inline negative prompt and runs every prompt in a prompts file rather than only the selected ones, so a notice says when the copied command differs from what Generate would run; an uploaded reference image is named by its file name, so replace it with the file's path.

Fields that take a path on the server's machine (prompt files, the output folder, checkpoints, LoRAs, reference images and source videos) have a folder button that opens a file browser inside the Web UI, so it works the same on every system and from a phone or another computer. It opens at the field's current path or at the matching folder (the output folder, ~/.ziv/models or ~/.ziv/loras), lists only the files that field accepts (Show all lists the rest), and keeps the last five choices under Recent. Click the path bar or press / to type a path; Hidden files shows names starting with a dot. Typing a path in the field itself suggests matching folders and files: Tab completes the first suggestion, the arrow keys and Enter pick another, and ↓ in an empty field suggests recent paths and the shortcut folders. The reference image also keeps an upload button for a picture on the device you're browsing from.

To give the preview more room, collapse the Compose and Settings sidebar with the « button next to Compose. It folds into a narrow strip with an expand button and a Generate button, and the choice is remembered in the browser. On phone-width screens the sidebar always shows above the preview.

While a job runs, its card shows the progress, the time left and a live preview of the current image. Pause and Cancel are at the top of the card; Skip and Repeat are next to the current image. Pause and Repeat wait until the current image is finished, while Skip and Cancel stop it at its next step. A video job offers Cancel only, plus Approve and Discard while it waits for a review (macOS); while its model loads, Cancel takes effect once loading finishes. If a job fails, the card shows why. Finished images appear in the history strip, newest first; scroll it to the end and older ones load in.

The workspace model picker and the Models page show whether each model is already downloaded; models that are not yet downloaded download on first use. They also show whether a downloaded model fits this machine's memory. On macOS this is compared with the GPU memory Apple recommends for the machine:

  • Fits: the estimate is at most 1.1 times the recommendation.
  • Tight: the estimate is at most 1.5 times the recommendation, which is MLX's default memory limit. The model runs, but macOS compresses or swaps other memory to make room, so the Mac can slow down while generating.
  • Too large: the estimate is above MLX's default memory limit. Expect heavy swapping that can make the whole Mac unresponsive, or an out-of-memory error.

On Windows and Linux the badges compare an image model with the GPU's memory and the machine's system memory (see Quantization):

  • Fits: the model fits comfortably.
  • Tight: the model runs, but slowly, because it does not fit in system memory or the GPU is nearly full.
  • Too large: the model needs more GPU memory than the GPU has. Try a lower quant.

The workspace badge follows the selected quantize level, so you can see whether q8 or q4 brings a large model within reach. Hover the badge for the estimate. After each job the Web UI returns the model's memory to the system.

Ideogram 4 (ideo) is selectable in the workspace model dropdown. When it is selected, the workspace offers a structured-JSON-caption input and a first-step-sigma control, while reference-image (img2img) and upscale are unavailable, and width and height are constrained to the 256–2048 range in multiples of 16.

docs.title: Keyboard shortcuts
docs.text:
Press ? anywhere outside a text field to see every shortcut. ⌘ on macOS is Ctrl elsewhere.

Anywhere:

Key Action ? Show all keyboard shortcuts G then W / P / G / M / C Go to Workspace / Prompts / Gallery / Models / Config

Workspace:

Key Action ⌘↵ Generate ⌘⇧↵ Generate with a new seed (re-rolls a locked seed) ⌘E Enhance the prompt Alt+1 / Alt+2 Focus the prompt / the settings (expands the sidebar) Alt+3 Focus the newest history tile (expands the strip; ← / → move between tiles) Alt+⇧+1 / Alt+⇧+2 Show or hide the sidebar (focuses the prompt / the settings when shown) Alt+⇧+3 Show or hide the history strip (focuses the newest tile when shown) Esc Esc Stop the running job (press twice) P Pause or resume the running job N Skip to the next image; during a review, discard the small render R Repeat the current image Y Approve the small render for upscaling (during a review)

Prompts:

Key Action ⌘S Save the prompt file ⌘Z Undo (outside text fields) ↵ Edit the focused prompt text or random choice $ Suggest snippets while editing a prompt ⌥↵ Edit the {a|b} choice at the caret, make one from the selected words, or start a new one (while editing) Esc / ⌘↵ Finish editing a prompt

Gallery:

Key Action Arrow keys Move between assets ↵ Open the viewer Space / X Select or deselect the focused asset ⌘A Select all loaded assets Delete / Backspace Delete the selection, or the focused asset (asks first) Esc Clear the selection

Full-screen asset viewer:

Key Action ← / → Previous / next asset Home / End First / last asset R Reuse settings E Use as reference: load an image as the reference image, together with its prompt. On a video, Extend: open it in the Extend Video tab D Download C Copy the prompt Delete / Backspace Delete (asks for confirmation: Enter confirms, Esc cancels) Shift+Delete Delete without asking I Toggle the details panel ? Show the viewer's shortcuts Esc Close the shortcut list, then the viewer

docs.title: Model Store (~/.ziv/)
docs.text:
Z-Vision Generator uses a central data directory for models and LoRAs:

~/.ziv/
├── models/    # Diffusers-format model directories
└── loras/     # LoRA .safetensors files

To add a model, copy (or symlink) the model directory into ~/.ziv/models/:

cp -r /path/to/my-model ~/.ziv/models/my-model

Then reference it by bare name:

ziv-image -m my-model --prompt "hello world"

docs.title: Resolution Order
docs.text:
When you pass -m <name> (both ziv-image and ziv-video):

  1. Path with / or \ → used as-is (local path)
  2. Bare name → checks ~/.ziv/models/<name>/ → uses it if found
  3. Alias → checks built-in and custom aliases (see Image Guide)
  4. Otherwise → treated as a HuggingFace repo ID (downloaded on first use)

Note: A local model directory at ~/.ziv/models/<name>/ takes priority over an alias with the same name.

LoRA generation inputs are local paths or bare names from ~/.ziv/loras/. To use a HuggingFace LoRA, import it first with ziv-model lora --hf ..., then reference the local LoRA name or path during generation.

docs.title: Download speed
docs.text:
Model downloads from HuggingFace use Xet. Set HF_XET_HIGH_PERFORMANCE=1 to let downloads try to saturate the network bandwidth and use all CPU cores. The variable is read when the program starts, so set it before launching ziv:

export HF_XET_HIGH_PERFORMANCE=1
ziv-image -m my-model --prompt "a landscape"

docs.title: ZIV_DATA_DIR Override
docs.text:
Set the ZIV_DATA_DIR environment variable to use a custom location instead of ~/.ziv/:

export ZIV_DATA_DIR=/mnt/fast-ssd/ziv
ziv-image -m my-model --prompt "a landscape"

docs.title: Error Log
docs.text: Each command records warnings and errors, with full tracebacks, in ~/.ziv/logs/<command>.log (ui.log, image.log, video.log or model.log). The file is cleared every time the command starts, so it only covers the latest run, and stays empty when nothing goes wrong. If the logs folder cannot be written, the log goes to the system temp folder instead; ziv ui prints the file's location at startup. Set ZIV_LOG=off to turn the log off.

docs.title: Linux: the terminal or editor closes while a model loads
docs.text:
On Linux distributions that run systemd-oomd, such as Ubuntu, loading a large model can close the terminal or editor that started the job, and the job with it, even when there is enough memory for the load to finish. systemd-oomd reacts to memory pressure (the time spent waiting for memory to be reclaimed), not to running out of memory. Loading 15–35 GB of weights on a machine with about 32 GB of RAM fills the page cache and can keep pressure above Ubuntu's limit of 50% for 20 seconds. oomd then stops the whole terminal or editor the job runs in. journalctl -u systemd-oomd lists each time it did.

To relax the limit for your user session, create /etc/systemd/system/user@.service.d/99-oomd-relax.conf with sudo:

[Service]
ManagedOOMMemoryPressureLimit=80%
ManagedOOMMemoryPressureDurationSec=60s
  • Apply: run sudo systemctl daemon-reload, then log out and back in, or reboot.
  • Verify: systemctl show user@$(id -u).service -p ManagedOOMMemoryPressureLimit prints 80%, and oomctl lists the new limit.
  • Revert: delete the file and repeat the reload and re-login.

80% for 60 seconds still stops runaway memory use, but lets typical model loads finish. The largest loads, such as Krea 2 without quantization, can still go over it; use -q 8 or -q 4 on these machines. ZVisionGenerator never changes this setting itself.

To protect your editor when oomd does act, start heavy jobs in their own unit, so oomd stops the job rather than the editor:

systemd-run --user --collect --same-dir -p OOMScoreAdjust=500 ziv-image -m my-model --prompt "a landscape"

docs.title: Image Generation Guide
docs.text:
Generate images from text prompts using ziv-image. Supports Z-Image / FLUX / Krea 2 models on macOS (Apple Silicon via mflux/MLX) and on Windows and Linux with NVIDIA GPUs via diffusers/CUDA, plus Ideogram 4 on all three.

On Windows and Linux, image generation requires CUDA to be visible to PyTorch. CPU fallback is not available for the diffusers image backend.

docs.title: Model Aliases
docs.text:
Built-in shorthands for common image models.

Alias Expands To zit Tongyi-MAI/Z-Image-Turbo klein4b black-forest-labs/FLUX.2-klein-4B klein9b black-forest-labs/FLUX.2-klein-9B ideo ideogram-ai/ideogram-4-fp8 (macOS), unsloth/ideogram-4-nf4-diffusers (Windows and Linux) krea2 unsloth/Krea-2-Turbo

For video aliases, see Video Guide → Supported Models.

ziv-image -m zit --prompt "a beautiful sunset"
ziv-image -m klein4b --prompt "a portrait"
ziv-image -m ideo --prompt "a portrait"
ziv-image -m krea2 -q 4 --prompt "a portrait"

docs.title: Ideogram 4
docs.text:
Ideogram 4 runs on macOS (Apple Silicon via mflux/MLX) and on Windows and Linux (NVIDIA GPU via diffusers/CUDA). It uses one model per platform, an FP8 one on macOS and an NF4 one on Windows and Linux (a 15 GB download), so quantization tiers do not apply: ziv-image rejects -q 4 / -q 8 for it, as the Web UI does. Width and height must be in the 256–2048 range and multiples of 16; size presets that exceed this range (for example --size xl with --ratio 16:9) are rejected before the model loads.

ziv-image -m ideo --prompt "a portrait"

Ideogram 4 does not support negative prompts or reference-image (img2img) steering; a negative prompt is dropped with a warning, and both --image and --upscale are rejected (each requires img2img, which Ideogram 4 does not support). LoRA weights work via --lora (and the Web UI's LoRA picker) on every platform. On Windows and Linux they load onto Ideogram 4's main transformer, so a LoRA made for its unconditional transformer is not supported, and a LoRA adds about 1 GB of GPU memory, so the largest sizes may then no longer fit.

Plain-text prompts are automatically wrapped into Ideogram 4's structured JSON caption format, so they generate without a plain-text caption warning while preserving the original wording. To supply a full structured JSON caption instead, pass it as the value of --json-prompt (mutually exclusive with --prompt): this skips random-choice {a|b|c} expansion and sends the caption verbatim. Without --json-prompt, {...} in a prompt is treated as random-choice syntax and corrupts a JSON caption. The --json-prompt value must be a valid JSON object, or generation is rejected before the model loads:

ziv-image -m ideo --json-prompt '{"high_level_description": "a portrait"}'

The automatic wrapper only repeats your prompt in the caption's fields, and Ideogram 4 often renders such sparse captions as a flat cut-out on a checkerboard background, especially posters and product shots. For a fuller caption, let the prompt enhancer write one: --enhance-format json, or Write as: JSON in the Enhance popover (see JSON Captions). The Smart enhancer writes better captions than Fast.

When neither --steps nor --guidance is given, Ideogram 4 uses its built-in tuned quality schedule. Supplying --steps and/or --guidance overrides that schedule with the explicit values.

The macOS model is gated on Hugging Face: accept its terms and log in (hf auth login) before the first download. The Windows and Linux model is downloaded from Unsloth's unmodified mirror of Ideogram's NF4 repo, pinned to a revision whose files were checked byte for byte against the official ones, so it needs no account. Either way the model is under Ideogram's non-commercial license, which applies as soon as you download or use it: see the LICENSE.md in the model folder. To use the official NF4 repo instead, pass -m ideogram-ai/ideogram-4-nf4-diffusers (it needs the login).

On Windows and Linux the model does not fit a consumer GPU at once, so the two transformers stream to the GPU block by block and the text encoder is on it only while it reads the prompt. On a 10 GB GPU with 32 GB of system memory, a 1024×1024 image with the default 20 steps takes about 2.5 minutes and peaks at about 6 GB of GPU memory and 20 GB of system memory; sizes up to about 1.8 megapixels (for example 1792×1024) work, taking longer, and larger ones (2048×1024 and up) run out of GPU memory. The first run also loads about 15 GB, which takes a minute or two.

Ideogram 4 sometimes returns a grey "Image blocked by safety filter" frame for harmless prompts. ZVisionGenerator adjusts the first denoising step slightly, which reduces these false positives without changing the prompt, seed or resolution. This is best-effort and not a way around the filter: prompts the filter actually objects to are still blocked. The adjustment defaults to a first-step sigma of 1.004 and can be overridden per run with --first-sigma (for example --first-sigma 1.005 or --first-sigma 1.006) when a harmless prompt is still blocked.

docs.title: In the Web UI
docs.text: Ideogram 4 is selectable in the workspace model dropdown. When it is selected, the workspace exposes a structured-JSON-caption input and a first-step-sigma control that mirror --json-prompt and --first-sigma. Reference-image (img2img) and upscale are unavailable for it, and width and height are constrained to the 256–2048 range in multiples of 16.

docs.title: Z-Image scheduler
docs.text: Z-Image uses the beta scheduler by default on every platform, so a prompt and seed look alike on macOS, Windows and Linux. Pass --scheduler with another name, or pick one in the Web UI, to change it for a run.

docs.title: Krea 2
docs.text:
krea2 is Krea 2 Turbo, a 12B text-to-image model distilled to 8 steps. The alias points to unsloth's ungated mirror of Krea's repo, so no Hugging Face token is needed; the weights are under the Krea 2 Community License. It defaults to 8 steps and guidance 1.0, which turns classifier-free guidance off; guidance above 1.0 turns it on, and each step then takes about twice as long. Negative prompts are turned off for Krea 2.

Krea 2 samples with its own schedule, so --scheduler is rejected for it and the Web UI hides the Scheduler control. Only Krea 2 Turbo and its fine-tunes are supported, not Krea 2 Raw.

The weights are large (about 26 GB for the transformer plus a 9 GB text encoder), so run it quantized on smaller machines:

  • macOS: -q 8 or -q 4. The text encoder is not quantized, so it adds about 9 GB at any level.
  • Windows and Linux: -q 8 needs about 18 GB of system memory and -q 4 fits 10–12 GB GPUs. Without quantization Krea 2 needs about 35 GB of system memory and is very slow on machines with less.

Reference images (--image), --upscale and LoRAs trained for Krea 2 (--lora) work on every platform.

docs.title: Custom Aliases
docs.text:
Add your own aliases in ~/.ziv/config.yaml:

model_aliases:
  mymodel: "my-org/my-model"

Note: A local model directory at ~/.ziv/models/<alias>/ overrides the alias.

View all aliases with:

ziv-model list

docs.title: Image Sizes
docs.text:
Default ratio is 2:3. Dimensions vary by --ratio.

Preset 1:1 16:9 9:16 3:2 2:3 xs 512×512 672×384 384×672 576×384 384×576 s 704×704 960×544 544×960 864×576 576×864 m 1024×1024 1344×768 768×1344 1216×832 832×1216 l 1408×1408 1920×1088 1088×1920 1728×1152 1152×1728 xl 1600×1600 2176×1216 1216×2176 1920×1280 1280×1920

Every preset keeps its exact size under --upscale 2; m, l and xl also do under --upscale 4.

Use -W / -H to override with exact pixel dimensions:

ziv-image -m my-model --prompt "a portrait" -W 1024 -H 1024

docs.title: Reference Image Steering
docs.text:
Use any image as a starting point — the model denoises it guided by your prompt.

ziv-image -m my-model --prompt "A woman in a red dress" --image photo.jpg --image-strength 0.4
ziv-image -m my-model --prompt "Cyberpunk cityscape" --image sketch.png --image-strength 0.8

The reference image is automatically resized to match target dimensions. Works on macOS, Windows, and Linux.

In the Web UI, Use as reference (E) in the asset viewer opens an image as the reference for img2img or img2vid and loads its prompt too, replacing an Enhanced prompt made for the previous one. For img2img the prompt goes into the Prompt box; for img2vid it goes into Scene, since it describes the first frame, and Action is left for what happens (see Scene and Action).

docs.title: LoRA Support
docs.text:
Both platforms support LoRA weights. Place .safetensors files in ~/.ziv/loras/:

# Single LoRA at default weight (1.0)
ziv-image -m my-model --lora myStyle

# Single LoRA with explicit weight
ziv-image -m my-model --lora myStyle:0.8

# Two LoRAs stacked
ziv-image -m my-model --lora style1:0.8,detail:0.5

Bare names are resolved from ~/.ziv/loras/. Full paths also work.

Standard LoRAs and LyCORIS LoKr files work on every platform and quantize level, and can be combined. Other LyCORIS formats are not supported; those parts of a file are skipped with a warning.

docs.title: Upscaling
docs.text:
The built-in upscale pipeline generates at a reduced size, then refines to target resolution:

  1. Generate at reduced size (target ÷ upscale factor)
  2. Lanczos upscale to target dimensions
  3. CAS pre-sharpening → img2img refinement → CAS post-sharpening
ziv-image -m my-model --prompt "a landscape" --upscale 2
ziv-image -m my-model --prompt "a landscape" --upscale 4 --upscale-denoise 0.3 --upscale-steps 8

# Use a different guidance for the upscale refine pass
ziv-image -m my-model --prompt "a landscape" --upscale 2 --upscale-guidance 0.8

# Skip the pre-sharpening CAS step before upscale refinement
ziv-image -m my-model --prompt "a landscape" --upscale 2 --no-upscale-sharpen

docs.title: Upscale Flags
docs.text: Flag Default Description --upscale disabled Upscale factor: 2 or 4 --upscale-denoise 0.3 (2×) / 0.4 (4×) Denoising strength for upscale pass --upscale-steps steps / 2 Refinement steps for upscale --upscale-guidance same as --guidance Override guidance scale for the upscale refine pass only --upscale-sharpen True CAS sharpening step before upscale refinement (--no-upscale-sharpen to disable) --upscale-save-pre False Save pre-upscale image alongside final

docs.title: Review before upscaling
docs.text:
With a review, each generation pauses after the small render, before the upscale. Approve upscales it; Discard skips the image and saves nothing. In the Web UI, turn on the Review row under Upscale and press Y to approve or N to discard. On the command line, add --review to --upscale. It needs a terminal and prints the path of the small render; press y to approve, n to discard or q to quit.

ziv-image -m my-model --prompt "a landscape" --upscale 2 --review

In a batch every image pauses. A Pause, Repeat or Next queued before the review still applies: pause and repeat take effect after the current image, and Next skips it.

docs.title: Upscaling an existing image (Web UI)
docs.text:
To upscale an image you already have, open the Upscale menu in the asset viewer (Gallery or Workspace) or the ⋯ menu on its thumbnail. Each option shows the output size, e.g. 2× → 1664×2432. The job runs in the Workspace job panel, or joins the queue when another job is running; starting it from the Gallery takes you there.

There are two kinds of upscale:

Menu item Available on What it does 2×, 4× macOS A plain upscale with SeedVR2: one step, no prompt, no image model. It enlarges the image faithfully and adds fine detail without redrawing it. 2× creative, 4× creative all platforms The image model redraws the enlarged image (img2img) with the image's own settings.

On Windows and Linux the menu shows only the creative items, labelled "creative". In the viewer, press X then 2 or 4 to run the plain upscale on macOS, or the creative one on Windows and Linux. The creative items on macOS are in the menu only.

docs.title: Plain upscale (macOS)
docs.text:
The plain upscale works for any image: files without recorded settings, imported files and images from models that cannot upscale or refine images (e.g. Ideogram 4). No image model needs to be configured, and the job panel notes "original settings unknown" for a file without a record. The result is saved as is, without the sharpen, contrast and saturation passes. A source that has a record carries its prompt, model and LoRAs over for Reuse settings.

  • Model. The app picks one SeedVR2 model for your Mac from its memory: the 7B model where an output of 16 megapixels (a 4× upscale of a 1 MP image) fits in memory, otherwise the 3B model. Both run at 8-bit. To force a model, set seedvr2.model (below).
  • First use. The job downloads the model (about 17 GB for 7B, 7.3 GB for 3B) and the job panel shows this as its own step. It then stores an 8-bit copy in the models folder (~/.ziv/models/) and removes the downloaded files to save disk, so the model keeps roughly half of its download size on disk. Later upscales load the copy. The Models page lists the model your Mac uses as seedvr2-7b@q8 (or seedvr2-3b@q8). Once the copy exists, the row shows its disk use and a delete button that removes it; the next plain upscale downloads the model again. That clean-up deletes the two downloaded files (the model's transformer and the shared VAE) from the shared Hugging Face cache, so they are removed even if another tool had cached them. If the chosen model changes (a seedvr2.model edit or a Mac with different memory), the previous model's copy stays in the hidden .seedvr2 folder inside the models folder and is not shown on the Models page; delete that folder by hand to reclaim the space.
  • Memory. A size that may need more memory than your Mac's GPU memory budget stays available, marked · high memory, and its tooltip says so. The job runs, but it can be slow while macOS swaps, and a size well beyond the budget may fail. Time grows about linearly with the output size: on a 32 GB M5 a 16 MP result took about 6 minutes. The plain upscale has no megapixel limit.

The model choice and its defaults live in the seedvr2 section of ~/.ziv/config.yaml; the values below are the defaults:

seedvr2:
  model: auto                  # auto, seedvr2-3b or seedvr2-7b
  softness: 0.75               # 0-1: pre-blur before upscaling; 0 = off
  reference_megapixels: 16     # Output size the automatic choice must fit (a typical 4x)
  tiers:                       # 8-bit, best first; the first that fits this Mac's memory at reference_megapixels is used
    - {model: seedvr2-7b, weights_gb: 9.26, activation_floor_gb: 10.79, activation_base_gb: 1.88, activation_gb_per_mp: 0.83}
    - {model: seedvr2-3b, weights_gb: 4.72, activation_floor_gb: 10.79, activation_base_gb: 1.10, activation_gb_per_mp: 0.89}

With model: auto the first tier whose estimate fits at reference_megapixels wins, and the last one runs when none does or the memory is unknown. A tier's estimate is weights_gb plus the larger of activation_floor_gb and activation_base_gb + activation_gb_per_mp × output megapixels; the same estimate decides which sizes are marked high memory. Set model to seedvr2-3b or seedvr2-7b to use only that model. softness sets how much the image is softened before SeedVR2 enlarges it; 0 turns that off. Config precedence applies as everywhere else.

docs.title: Creative upscale
docs.text:
The image is resized, refined with img2img and sharpened, using the settings recorded in the file: prompt, model, seed, steps, guidance, scheduler, LoRAs, negative prompt and quantization. When the recorded model is not configured here, the default image model refines it with its own defaults. Images without recorded settings (imported or older files) are refined by the default image model with an empty prompt; the job panel notes this. The image is already sharpened, so by default the CAS pass before refinement is skipped (sharpening.existing_pre_upscale: 0); the final pass uses sharpening.existing_upscaled. Contrast and saturation are not applied again.

Both kinds save the result next to the original as <name>_2x.png or <name>_4x.png, with a counter (_2) if that name exists. A creative option is disabled, with the reason in its tooltip, when the model cannot upscale or refine images (e.g. Ideogram 4), or when the output would exceed the model's maximum dimension or the megapixel limit. These settings live in the upscale section of ~/.ziv/config.yaml:

upscale:
  existing_denoise_small: 0.4      # Refinement denoise for outputs up to existing_large_megapixels
  existing_denoise_large: 0.2      # Larger outputs: high denoise at large sizes invents detail and seams
  existing_large_megapixels: 2
  max_megapixels: 20               # Largest output a viewer upscale may produce

The denoise depends on the output size, not the factor, so upscaling an upscale (2× then 2×) refines as lightly as a direct 4× to the same size.

default_denoise_2x and default_denoise_4x apply to --upscale and the Workspace upscale settings only.

docs.title: Quantization
docs.text:
Reduces memory usage and speeds up generation at the cost of some quality.

Platform Levels Method macOS 4-bit, 8-bit mflux quantization Windows / Linux 4-bit, 8-bit NF4 (bitsandbytes) and FP8 
ziv-image -m my-model -q 4    # 4-bit quantization
ziv-image -m my-model -q 8    # 8-bit quantization

On macOS, memory is shared between the CPU and GPU, so an unquantized model larger than the machine's recommended GPU memory makes macOS compress or swap other memory, and well beyond it the whole system swaps heavily. On a 16 GB Mac, for example, Z-Image Turbo and FLUX.2 Klein need -q 8 or -q 4. The Web UI's memory badge shows which levels fit.

On Windows and Linux:

  • Unquantized and -q 8 keep the model in system memory and move it to the GPU piece by piece, so they need only about 4 GB of GPU memory. -q 8 halves the system memory a model needs, which makes large models much faster on machines that cannot hold them unquantized.
  • -q 4 keeps the whole model on the GPU, so the GPU must hold the model at 4 bits (Krea 2: about 7 GB).

The prompt enhancer is unloaded before the model loads, so Enhance each image does not add to the model's memory.

docs.title: Stored quants
docs.text:
The first time a model runs at -q 8 or -q 4 (or Quant: q8/q4 in the Web UI), its quantized weights are saved in ~/.ziv/models/ as <name>@q8 or <name>@q4, where <name> is the installed model or the alias you picked (for example zit@q8). Later jobs load that copy instead of quantizing again, so they start faster and do not briefly need the unquantized model's memory. The first job shows Saving a q8 copy…; the copy needs roughly half (q8) or a quarter (q4) of the model's disk space.

  • macOS: the first job takes about 20–30 seconds longer.

  • Windows and Linux: the first job takes a few minutes longer.

  • The copy holds the base model only. LoRAs are applied on top of it when a job loads.

  • It is replaced automatically when the source model's weights change (including a new download of an alias's Hugging Face repo) or the software that creates it is updated. After an update that changes the quantization code (for example a new mflux version on macOS), the next q8 or q4 job of each model rebuilds its copy once, which takes the extra time and disk space of a first run.
  • It is listed on the Models page as q8 copy of <name>, where you can delete it to free disk space. It does not appear in the model picker: choose the base model and a quantize level.
  • Deleting a model on the Models page, or an alias's Hugging Face download, also deletes its copies.
  • Stopping a job while the copy is being saved takes effect once the current save step finishes. The copy is then discarded and the next job tries again.
  • An alias whose model is not downloaded yet is downloaded first, and the copy is saved once the download is complete (on Windows and Linux, a q8 copy is saved by the next job).
  • A model given as a raw Hugging Face repo id or a folder outside ~/.ziv/models/ (-m org/repo, -m /path/to/model) is quantized at load each time. Use an alias, or install the model, to get a copy.

You can also save a quantized copy when converting a checkpoint (ziv-model model … --quantize 8, or Quantized Copy on the Models page).

docs.title: Contrast
docs.text:
ziv-image -m my-model --prompt "a sunset" --contrast 1.2        # boost contrast (1.0 = no change)
ziv-image -m my-model --prompt "a sunset" --no-contrast         # disable entirely

docs.title: Saturation
docs.text:
ziv-image -m my-model --prompt "a sunset" --saturation 1.3       # boost saturation (1.0 = no change)
ziv-image -m my-model --prompt "a sunset" --no-saturation        # disable entirely

docs.title: Sharpening
docs.text:
ziv-image -m my-model --prompt "a sunset" --sharpen              # enabled by default
ziv-image -m my-model --prompt "a sunset" --sharpen 0.6          # custom amount (0.0–1.5)
ziv-image -m my-model --prompt "a sunset" --no-sharpen           # disable

Without an amount, the final pass uses the config: sharpening.normal for plain images and sharpening.upscaled for upscaled ones (sharpening.pre_upscale is the pass before upscale refinement). In the Web UI, leave the Sharpen amount empty (auto) to use these, or type an amount to override them. Amounts above 1.5 are rejected: the filter breaks down beyond that.

sharpening:
  normal: 1.0
  upscaled: 1.2
  pre_upscale: 0.8
  existing_upscaled: 1.2     # final pass when upscaling an existing image (viewer)
  existing_pre_upscale: 0    # before refining an existing image; 0 = off

The asset viewer's Details show the amounts an image was made with, including the pre-sharpen of an upscale.

docs.title: Output Files
docs.text:
Images are saved as <set name>_<YYYY-MM-DD_HH-MM-SS>.png (for example portrait_2026-10-04_14-03-22.png), with _2, _3… added when that name is already taken, so no file is overwritten. Videos follow the same pattern with their format's extension.

The settings each file was made with are embedded in it: prompt, negative prompt, model and family, seed, steps, guidance, scheduler, size, LoRAs, reference image and strength, quantization, generation time, upscale factor, method (seedvr2 or creative) and the settings it used (model and softness for SeedVR2; denoise and steps for creative), and the sharpen, contrast and saturation amounts. The Web UI asset viewer shows them under Details (I), and Reuse settings loads them into the Workspace. Paths inside your home folder, such as LoRAs, models and reference images, are recorded as ~/…, so a shared file does not show your user name; the prompt is stored as written.

docs.title: Keyboard Shortcuts
docs.text:
During batch generation:

Key Action Description n Skip Stop current image, move to next prompt q Quit Stop current image, exit batch p Pause Finish current image, pause until keypress r Repeat Finish current image, re-run the same prompt (same random choices and enhanced prompt) with a new random seed

The keys also work while prompts are enhanced and while the model loads. During enhancement, n skips the current rewrite, q stops before the model loads, p pauses, and r has no effect. See While Prompts Are Enhanced.

In the Web UI, image job controls appear only while the backend reports that the running job supports them.

docs.title: Related Guides
docs.text: • Prompts Guide — prompt files, variables, structured prompts, and snippets

docs.title: Model & LoRA Management
docs.text: The ziv-model command converts checkpoints, imports LoRAs, and lists installed assets.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
ziv-model has three subcommands:

  • model — convert safetensors checkpoints to diffusers format
  • lora — import LoRA files from local paths or HuggingFace
  • list — show installed models, video models, LoRAs, and aliases

docs.title: Converting Models (model subcommand)
docs.text:
Convert safetensors checkpoints to diffusers format, stored in ~/.ziv/models/.

# Convert a Z-Image checkpoint (output: ~/.ziv/models/<name>/)
ziv-model model -i checkpoint.safetensors --name my-model

# Convert a FLUX.2 Klein 4B checkpoint
ziv-model model -i klein4b.safetensors --name klein4b --model-type flux2-klein-4b

# Copy base model files instead of symlinking
ziv-model model -i checkpoint.safetensors --name my-model --copy

# Also save a q8 copy (~/.ziv/models/my-model@q8/), used whenever my-model runs at -q 8 (macOS)
ziv-model model -i checkpoint.safetensors --name my-model --quantize 8

docs.title: model Flags
docs.text:
Flag Default Description -i, --input (required) Path to .safetensors checkpoint --name input filename Custom model folder name --model-type zimage Model type: zimage, flux2-klein-4b, flux2-klein-9b, krea2-turbo --base-model Tongyi-MAI/Z-Image-Turbo Base HF repo (only for zimage type) --copy off Copy files instead of symlinking --quantize off Also save a quantized copy as <name>@q4 or <name>@q8 (4 or 8); see Stored quants

Checkpoints can be bfloat16, float16, float32, or FP8. Scaled FP8 checkpoints (for example ComfyUI FP8 exports, which store a weight_scale next to each weight) are dequantized to bfloat16 during conversion. Block-wise or other quantized formats (such as NVFP4) are not supported.

krea2-turbo converts a fine-tune of Krea 2 Turbo. Native Krea 2 and ComfyUI checkpoints are both accepted, and a bundled text encoder or VAE is ignored; the text encoder and VAE come from unsloth's ungated mirror unsloth/Krea-2-Turbo.

Ideogram 4 is used via the ideo alias or a local FP8 (macOS) or NF4 (Windows and Linux) model directory and is distributed ready-to-use. It has no checkpoint-convert path, so it is not a --model-type option.

docs.title: Importing LoRAs (lora subcommand)
docs.text:
Import LoRA .safetensors files into ~/.ziv/loras/ from local paths or HuggingFace.

# Import a local LoRA file
ziv-model lora -i /path/to/style.safetensors --name my-style

# Download a LoRA from HuggingFace
ziv-model lora --hf user/lora-repo --name my-lora

# Download a specific file from a multi-file HF repo
ziv-model lora --hf user/lora-repo --file model.safetensors

docs.title: lora Flags
docs.text: Flag Default Description -i, --input — Path to local .safetensors file (mutually exclusive with --hf) --hf — HuggingFace repo ID (mutually exclusive with -i) --file auto-detect Specific .safetensors file in the HF repo --name filename stem Custom LoRA name

docs.title: Listing Assets (list subcommand)
docs.text:
Show installed models, video models, LoRAs, and model aliases.

# List everything
ziv-model list

# Show only models
ziv-model list --models

# Show only LoRAs
ziv-model list --loras

docs.title: list Flags
docs.text: Flag Default Description --models off Show only models --loras off Show only LoRAs

docs.title: Managing Models in the Web UI
docs.text:
The Web UI's Models page lists the same models and LoRAs and can convert checkpoints and import LoRAs. Each row also has a delete button, which asks for confirmation first and is unavailable while generation jobs are running or queued:

  • Converted models (in ~/.ziv/models/): deletes the model folder. Base-model files it links to in the HuggingFace cache are kept.
  • HuggingFace models (aliases such as klein9b): deletes the model's download from the HuggingFace cache. The alias stays, and the model downloads again the next time you use it. If converted models link to files in that download, the confirmation lists them, because they stop working until it is downloaded again. The button appears once the model's files are fully downloaded.
  • LoRAs (in ~/.ziv/loras/): deletes the .safetensors file.
  • SeedVR2 upscale model (macOS): the image upscale model has a row of its own, seedvr2-7b@q8 or seedvr2-3b@q8 depending on your Mac's memory, with its download size. Once the first plain upscale has stored it, the row shows its disk use and a delete button that removes that stored copy. Nothing else is affected, and the next plain upscale downloads the model again. See Upscaling an existing image.

docs.title: Prompts Guide
docs.text: Z-Vision Generator supports inline prompts, YAML prompt files with batch generation, prompt variables, structured prompts, and reusable snippets. This guide covers the full prompts system used by both ziv-image and ziv-video.

docs.title: Inline Prompts
docs.text:
Use --prompt for quick, one-off generation:

ziv-image -m my-model --prompt "a beautiful sunset over the ocean"
ziv-video -m ltx-4 --prompt "A cat walking through a garden"

When --prompt is provided, it overrides --prompts-file.

docs.title: Prompt Files
docs.text:
Use --prompts-file (or -p) to load prompts from a YAML file. The default file is prompts.yaml.

ziv-image -m my-model -p prompts.yaml -r 3
ziv-image -m my-model -p my-prompts.yaml

Each entry has a set name and a list of prompt objects:

gorilla:
  - active: False
    prompt: |
      A gorilla. Detailed fur.
      In a jungle. Rainy day. Moody lighting.

woman:
  - active: True
    prompt: |
      30yo woman, in red dress.
      Walking down a city street. Evening.
  • active: True (default) — prompt is generated. active: False — skipped.
  • Multiple prompts per set are supported.
  • The set name becomes the output filename prefix.

In the Web UI, choose Prompt file as the prompt source and type or browse to a YAML file on the machine running the server. Compose then summarizes the selected prompts; click Prompts… (or the summary) to open the chooser, where you can filter prompts, select whole sets with All/None, expand a prompt to see its negative prompt, and confirm with Use N prompts. ✨ Enhance sets the options for Enhance each image when generating, and Edit opens the file on the Prompts page. If you edit the path manually, the visible value is the value submitted; use Enter or Browse when you want the UI to inspect the file and refresh the option list before generating.

docs.title: Prompt Builder (Web UI)
docs.text:
The Web UI's Prompts page (G then P) builds prompt files without typing YAML. It reads and writes the same file the CLI uses, and keeps the file's comments, quoting and | blocks.

  • Snippets (left) are listed with how often each is used; unused ones are dimmed. Click one to edit it, ＋ to add one, and drag one onto a prompt to add a $reference. Renaming a snippet updates every reference to it.
  • Sets (centre) are panels of prompts, one row each. Rename a set in place (the name starts the output filenames), add prompts with ＋, and use a set's ⋯ menu to duplicate, move, turn all prompts on or off, or delete it.
  • Entries show $snippets as chips (red when undefined) and {a|b} choices as pills. Click the text, or press ↵ on it, to edit; typing $ suggests snippet names. Click a pill to edit its options, one per line; an empty line is an empty option. While typing, put the caret in a choice and press ⌥↵ (or Edit choice under the text) to edit it the same way, select words and press ⌥↵ (Make a random choice) to turn them into a choice, or press ⌥↵ anywhere else (New random choice) to type the options of a new choice at the caret, one per line. The options box takes focus; ⌘↵ applies and Esc cancels, both returning you to the prompt. Each prompt has an active switch and ✨ Enhance: off, the default options (enhance: true), or chosen style, mood, details, length and motion (motion applies to video only). Its popover also has the Rewrite choice (Scene and action, or Action only) for video entries, saved as parts:. Its ⋯ menu adds or removes a negative prompt, and duplicates, moves or deletes the prompt.
  • Text / Fields switches a prompt between plain text and named fields (a structured prompt). Switching to fields puts the text in one field for you to name; a field without a name is a problem until you name it. Lists and nested values that the builder can't edit are shown flattened and kept exactly as written; Convert to text replaces one with its flattened text.
  • Drag a set or an entry by its ⠿ grip to reorder it; drop an entry on another set's header to move it there. The menus offer the same moves.
  • Preview (right) shows the selected entry as the model receives it, with snippets resolved and fields flattened, its prompt id, its enhancement and its problems. 🎲 Roll picks one option of every choice, as a run would.
  • ▶ (Generate this one) saves the file, then queues that one prompt with the current Workspace settings. Your prompt selection in the Workspace doesn't change. Use in Workspace saves and selects the file there.

Saving (⌘S) is blocked while the file has errors that would stop it from loading (an undefined snippet in an active entry, an empty prompt, two sets with the same name); the Save button says what to fix.
