Warnings, such as an invalid enhance: block, don't block saving. Saving keeps the prompts selected in the Workspace pointing at the same entries, even when you reorder, move or rename them.

⌘Z undoes changes back to the last save. Unsaved changes are kept in the browser, so leaving the page or reloading doesn't lose them; reopening the file offers to restore them. If the file changed on disk since you opened it (for example in another editor), saving asks before overwriting it.

A file that isn't valid YAML, or isn't shaped like a prompt file, opens in a repair view with the error and the raw text to fix. New file… in the file menu creates an empty prompt file in a folder you choose.

docs.title: Prompt Variables
docs.text:
Use {option1|option2|option3} syntax for random selection each run:

"A {red|blue} car"                         → "A red car" or "A blue car"
"A {big|small} {red|blue} {car|truck}"     → random combo each run
"{Nikon Z9 {50mm|35mm}|Canon EOS 5D}"     → nesting resolves inside-out

Variables are resolved independently each run, so repeated runs (-r 3) produce different combinations. The {a|b|c} random choice syntax works within structured prompt values too.

Pass a JSON object as the value of --json-prompt (mutually exclusive with --prompt) to provide a literal structured JSON caption inline. The value opts out of {a|b|c} expansion and is sent verbatim (used for Ideogram 4). It must be a valid JSON object, or generation is rejected before the model loads.

docs.title: Structured Prompts
docs.text:
The prompt (and negative) field accepts dicts, lists, and nested combinations — not just strings. Structured values are flattened into a single prompt string with ". " as separator. Dict keys become prefixes; list items are joined.

diner_scene:
  - prompt:
      Subjects:
        - Lisa: An old lady with grey hair and kind eyes
        - George is a retired professor with round glasses
        - Nina:
            Hair: Tidy
            Clothes: Red dress
      Setting: Lisa, Nina and George are sharing a meal at the diner
      Style:
        Camera: iPhone
        Color: Warm

This flattens to:

Subjects: Lisa: An old lady with grey hair and kind eyes. George is a retired professor
with round glasses. Nina: Hair: Tidy. Clothes: Red dress. Setting: Lisa, Nina and George
are sharing a meal at the diner. Style: Camera: iPhone. Color: Warm

Prompts can be plain strings, dicts, lists, or nested combinations.

docs.title: Flattening Rules
docs.text:
• Strings are used as-is.
  • Lists have each item flattened and joined with ". ".
  • Dicts produce "key: value" pairs joined with ". ". Nested dicts/lists are recursively flattened.

docs.title: Snippets
docs.text:
Define reusable prompt fragments under a reserved snippets top-level key in your prompts file:

snippets:
  nina:
    Hair: Tidy
    Clothes: Red dress
  warm_style:
    Camera: iPhone
    Color: Warm
  diner: a cozy 1950s American diner with checkered floors

Reference a snippet with $name:

diner_scene:
  - prompt:
      Subjects:
        - Nina: $nina
      Setting: Lisa and Nina are sharing a meal at $diner
      Style: $warm_style
  • Standalone $nina (the entire value) preserves structure — the dict is kept as-is for flattening.
  • Inline $diner within a string is flattened and substituted in place.
  • Snippets can reference other snippets.
  • Circular references are detected and raise an error.

The snippets key is not treated as a prompt set — it is consumed during loading and removed.

docs.title: Negative Prompts
docs.text:
The negative field in a prompt object specifies what the model should avoid:

portrait:
  - prompt: "A woman in a garden"
    negative: "blurry, low quality, bad anatomy"

Note: FLUX.2 models do not support negative prompts. If a negative prompt is provided with a FLUX.2 model, a warning is issued and the negative prompt is ignored.

The negative field supports the same structured format as prompt (strings, dicts, lists).

docs.title: Scenes for Video
docs.text:
A video prompt can have a scene (who and where, look, style, camera setup) apart from its action. Add scene: to an entry:

snippets:
  courtyard: A knight in a grey castle courtyard, overcast, handheld camera.

castle:
  - scene: $courtyard
    prompt: She draws her sword and turns to the gate.
  - scene: $courtyard
    prompt: She sheathes the sword and walks toward the tower.
  - prompt: A raven lands on the wall.   # no scene: uses --scene or the Workspace Default scene
  • scene: belongs to an entry. To share one scene across a set, put it in a $snippet as above; there is no scene on the set itself.
  • The video model receives the scene first, then the prompt. An entry with no scene: uses --scene (or the Workspace's Default scene) if one is given, and otherwise only its prompt.
  • A scene: takes snippets, structured values and {a|b} choices like a prompt does. An entry still needs a prompt.
  • Image jobs ignore scene:, so a file can serve both.
  • Old prompt files work unchanged.

With --extend, each entry's prompt is the action that follows the source clip, and an entry's scene: replaces the source's scene for that entry (see Extend a Video).

docs.title: Enhancing Prompts
docs.text:
A small local LLM can rewrite a prompt with more visual detail before it is generated. It runs on your machine. The default model is an uncensored variant of Qwen3.5-4B, because small instruction-tuned models often refuse or tone down ordinary creative prompts, such as a battle scene, a horror shot or a villain's portrait. The uncensored variant rewrites them faithfully instead.

There are two built-in models. Fast is the default. Smart is larger and follows your options and wording more closely (it keeps counts, adds fewer things you did not ask for, and writes better JSON captions), but needs more memory and a larger download.

Platform Enhancer Model First-use download Needs macOS Fast McG-221/Qwen3.5-4B-heretic-mlx-4Bit (mlx-lm, 4-bit) ≈2.4 GB macOS Smart TheCluster/Qwen3.5-27B-Heretic-MLX-4bit (mlx-lm, 4-bit) ≈16 GB about 20 GB of GPU memory (a Mac with 32 GB) Windows / Linux Fast coder3101/Qwen3.5-4B-heretic (transformers, 4-bit on CUDA) ≈9 GB Windows / Linux Smart coder3101/Qwen3.5-9B-heretic (transformers, 4-bit on CUDA) ≈19 GB about 9 GB of GPU memory

Choose Fast or Smart under Enhancer in the Enhance popover, or pass --enhance-model smart on the command line. The choice applies to the whole job. On a machine where Smart does not fit (too little GPU memory, or no NVIDIA GPU on Windows or Linux), the popover shows why and Smart cannot be picked; on the command line a warning says so and Fast runs. Downloaded models stay in the Hugging Face cache; delete them there to free the disk space.

Without a CUDA GPU, Windows and Linux run the enhancer on the CPU: it works, but each rewrite can take a few minutes and about 10 GB of RAM. The status line says so when this happens. If the machine has an NVIDIA GPU, a warning also suggests updating its driver to 580 or newer, the usual reason CUDA is missing.

All built-in models are pinned to a revision. To use another chat model, set Prompt Enhancer Model on the Config page to a Hugging Face owner/name (optionally owner/name@revision) or a local folder; it then replaces the Fast/Smart choice. --enhance-model REPO[@REVISION] does the same for one run. Thinking-tuned or heavily merged models are slower and follow the length and style options less reliably.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Option Choose Values Style one Keep, Photographic, Candid, Street photography, Analog film, Black & white, Studio portrait, Product shot, Cinematic, Illustration, Anime, Comic, 3D render, Painterly Mood one Keep, Serene, Joyful, Romantic, Melancholic, Mysterious, Eerie, Dramatic, Epic, Whimsical, Nostalgic Details any Lighting, Composition, Camera & lens, Materials & textures, Color & mood, Environment, Subject Motion (video only) any Action / sequence, Camera movement, Pacing Sound (video with audio on) any Ambience, Sound effects, Dialogue, Music Length one Shorter (≈50 %), Same, Longer (≈200 %), Extra long (≈300 %) Direction free text e.g. at night, in the rain or focus on the dog (up to 300 characters)

Mood sets the feeling of the scene. The enhancer conveys it through light, color, setting and expression instead of naming it. The Color & mood detail only adds more description of color and mood; it does not pick one.

Length is a target, not a guarantee. Longer aims for at least 40 words and Extra long for at least 80, so short prompts still grow; Shorter never aims below 12 words, so a prompt of 12 words or fewer keeps about the same length. Results are capped at 300 words (180 for FLUX.1, whose text encoder reads fewer tokens); when a prompt is already at the cap, it keeps about the same length. On short prompts, Same is approximate.

The enhancer keeps your subject and every detail you describe. It adds only things that can be seen, no smells or story, and never adds new people, animals, or major objects. Sound is the exception for video with audio on:

  • The enhancer keeps every sound and every quoted line of speech you wrote, word for word, whether or not a Sound option is picked.
  • With no Sound option picked, it adds no new sounds.
  • Ambience and Sound effects describe the setting's soundscape and sounds that match the action. Music describes music in the scene or a score.
  • Dialogue keeps your quoted lines. If you wrote none, it writes short lines that fit the scene. Only people already in the scene speak.
  • With audio off, and for images, the enhancer describes no sounds and Sound is ignored.

Direction is a short instruction the enhancer follows, such as a time of day, weather, or what to focus on. A direction alone is enough to enhance, without picking other options.

The enhancer also knows the job's shape:

  • Frame: portrait, landscape or square, from the ratio or size, so the composition fits the frame.
  • Clip length (video): one continuous action for clips up to 5 seconds, two or three beats up to 10 seconds, so the action fits the clip.
  • Starting image: for image-to-video, the rewrite describes motion and change instead of appearance, which the first frame already shows. For img2img it mentions the subject only briefly. The enhancer does not see the image itself.

docs.title: Scene and Action (Video)
docs.text:
For video, one rewrite returns two parts: a scene and an action (see Scenes for Video). The options shape them differently:

Option Shapes Style, Mood, Details mostly the scene Motion, Sound the action Direction both
  • Text to video splits and expands, so it works when you wrote everything in the prompt or gave only a scene: the setting, look and camera setup go to the scene, and events in time order, camera moves, sound and quoted dialogue go to the action.
  • Image to video keeps your scene (what the image shows) and writes only the action by default. With a blank scene, or with Rewrite set to Scene and action, it writes a short scene (style, and what the image does not show) and an action that describes the change.
  • Extend writes the action that happens next, using the previous clip's prompt as context so it does not repeat its actions or spoken lines. From a clip made without a scene, the enhancer takes a scene from the old prompt. See Extend a Video.
  • Length applies to the scene and the action together.
  • If the enhancer does not return a scene and an action, it tries once more, then uses its rewrite as the action and keeps your scene, with a warning.

docs.title: Rewrite: scene and action, or action only
docs.text:
The Rewrite option (parts in the CLI and prompt files) chooses what the enhancer writes:

Rewrite parts What you get Scene and action both A rewritten scene and a rewritten action. With no scene, the enhancer splits your text into both. Action only action Your scene is kept exactly as written. The enhancer reads it and writes an action that fits it.
  • The default depends on the workflow: Extend Video rewrites the action only when the clip has a scene, so a chain of extensions keeps its look, and Image to Video does the same when it has a scene, so the scene that describes the starting image is not restyled. Text to Video rewrites both.
  • Style, Mood and Details shape the scene, so they have no effect while Rewrite is Action only. Motion, Sound, Length and Direction still shape the action.
  • With Action only and a scene, Enhance always rewrites the action, even when every other option is left at "keep".
  • Action only needs a scene. With a blank scene, Action only is unavailable in the Web UI, and the run rewrites both parts. On the command line it does the same and warns once.
  • Image workflows ignore Rewrite.

docs.title: JSON Captions (Ideogram 4)
docs.text:
Ideogram 4 reads structured JSON captions (see Ideogram 4). With ideo, the Enhance popover has a Write as choice: Text rewrites your prompt as usual, JSON writes a full caption from it instead, with a summary, the look, lighting and colors, the background, one element per thing you named, and the lettering you asked for.

  • The same options apply: Style decides photo or artwork, Mood shapes the look and colors, Details and Length decide how much is described, and Direction is followed.
  • Quoted text ("OPEN", 'LISBOA', 「パン屋」) and names after called or named become text elements, copied exactly. On a card or logo, words you wrote without quotes are used too. Signs you mention without their words may get short words that fit, in the language you name.
  • The caption appears in the Enhanced tab, laid out for reading, and Generate sends it as the structured caption. Edit it there like any Enhanced text.
  • With Enhance each image when generating, every image gets its own caption.
  • If the enhancer returns no usable caption twice, the run reports it and keeps your prompt.
  • Smart writes noticeably better captions than Fast.

On the command line use --enhance-format json; it needs a model that takes JSON captions. With --prompt it turns on enhancement by itself. With a prompt file it writes captions for the entries that have their own enhance:, keeping their settings, as the Web UI does without auto-enhance; add --enhance to rewrite every prompt with the same settings.

docs.title: In the Web UI
docs.text:
• Enhance: click ✨ Enhance in the prompt box, pick options, and click Enhance prompt. The rewrite appears in the Enhanced tab. The button is unavailable while generation jobs are running or queued. Enhance again always starts from your text, and Clear empties the Enhanced text.
  • Video has a Rewrite choice first in the popover: Scene and action or Action only (see Rewrite). The tabs are Your text and Enhanced, and each holds a Scene and an Action box (the Prompt box of a video is called Action) that switch together. The Rewrite choice is remembered for each video workflow.
  • Each part decides on its own. For the Scene and for the Action, Generate sends the Enhanced text when that part's Enhanced box has text, and your text otherwise. With Action only, the Enhanced Scene stays empty ("Not enhanced. Generate uses your scene.") and editing your Scene applies directly. Both Enhanced boxes are editable, and typing into an empty one makes that text the part's enhanced text.
  • A part that sends its Enhanced text shows Uses enhanced beside its label in both tabs, with Use mine, which empties that Enhanced box so Generate uses your text again. The Enhanced tab shows used while either Enhanced box has text.
  • If you change the scene or action, or switch workflows, afterwards, the Enhanced text is marked Out of date, and each part that uses enhanced text shows the badge too. It is still used until you choose Use mine, Re-enhance or Clear. Putting the text back, for example with Use the clip's scene when extending, clears the badge.
  • {a|b} choices are picked before the rewrite, so the enhancer sees one plain prompt and the Enhanced prompt has no choices left. Enhance again for a different pick, or use Enhance each image when generating to keep a fresh pick per image.
  • Enhance each image when generating rewrites every image's prompt on the server, after its {a|b} choices are picked, using that image's seed. It works with inline prompts and prompt files. All rewrites run before the model loads, so the first image starts once every prompt is rewritten; the progress panel shows Enhancing prompt N of M. A prompt that could not be enhanced, or was skipped, is marked in the panel and generated from the original prompt.
  • Enhance is unavailable while a job runs.

docs.title: In Prompt Files and the CLI
docs.text:
Add enhance: to an entry to enhance it on every run:

woman:
  - prompt: 30yo woman in red dress walking down a city street, evening
    enhance:
      style: cinematic
      mood: mysterious
      details: [lighting, camera]
      length: longer
      note: rain on the pavement
  - prompt: a quiet street at dawn
    enhance: true        # default options
  - prompt: two friends talking at a cafe table
    enhance:
      sound: [ambient, dialogue]   # video with audio on
  - scene: A fisherman on a wooden pier at dawn, mist over the water.
    prompt: he casts his line
    enhance:
      parts: action                # video: keep the scene, rewrite only the action

An entry's own enhance: that asks for no change at all (style and mood keep, no details, length same, no motion or sound, no direction) is refused when the file loads: a warning appears and that entry is not enhanced. To have the enhancer split a single prompt into scene and action, use enhance: true or set at least one option. Job-level --enhance and the Web UI accept keep-all settings when the prompt has no scene. parts: action counts as a change, so an entry with it is kept even when every other option keeps things as they are.

From the command line, --enhance enhances every prompt and overrides entries' enhance: settings; --no-enhance turns all enhancement off:

ziv-image -m klein9b --prompt "a fox in snow" --enhance
ziv-image -m klein9b -p prompts.yaml --enhance style=photo,mood=serene,details=lighting+camera,length=longer
ziv-video -m ltx-8 --prompt "a fox runs" --enhance style=cinematic,motion=action+camera-move,sound=ambient+effects
ziv-video -m ltx-8 --scene "A fox in a snowy birch forest at dawn." --prompt "it runs" --enhance parts=action
ziv-image -m klein9b --prompt "a lighthouse" --enhance-note "in a storm, at night"
ziv-image -m klein9b --prompt "a fox in snow" --enhance --enhance-model smart
ziv-image -m ideo --prompt "a travel poster for Lisbon with the text 'LISBOA'" --enhance-format json
ziv-image -m klein9b -p prompts.yaml --no-enhance

--enhance-note sets the direction and turns on enhancement by itself.

motion and sound only apply to video, and sound only with audio on. Prompt files shared between image and video may include them; images ignore them.

The enhanced prompt is printed while prompts are enhanced and again before each generation, and stored in the image or video metadata, so Gallery shows and reuses the prompt that actually rendered.

docs.title: While Prompts Are Enhanced
docs.text:
Jobs with auto enhancement rewrite every prompt before the model loads. In image jobs (Web UI controls or ziv-image keys):

  • Next (n) skips the current rewrite; that image uses the original prompt.
  • Quit (q) stops the job before the model loads.
  • Pause (p) waits until you resume.
  • Repeat (r) has no effect.

Web UI video jobs offer only Cancel, which also stops the rewrites; ziv-video can be stopped with Ctrl+C.

Repeat and automatic retries keep the image's {a|b} choices and enhanced prompt and only change the seed. The new seed is always random, even when a seed is set.

docs.title: Memory
docs.text: The enhancer and the image or video model are never loaded together: the enhancer is unloaded, and its memory freed, before the model loads. Peak memory is the larger of the two, not their sum. Clicking Enhance loads the enhancer (about 3 GB on macOS) and frees it after two idle minutes, or when a job starts.

docs.title: Combining Variables with Structured Prompts
docs.text:
Variables work inside structured prompt values, so you can create prompts with controlled randomness:

character:
  - prompt:
      Subject: "A {young|old} {man|woman} with {red|blonde|dark} hair"
      Setting: "{A park|A cafe|A beach} on a {sunny|rainy} day"
      Style:
        Camera: "{Nikon Z9|Canon EOS 5D}"
        Color: "{Warm|Cool|Neutral}"

docs.title: Organizing Large Prompt Files
docs.text:
• Use descriptive set names — they become output filename prefixes.
  • Use active: False to temporarily disable prompts without deleting them.
  • Extract common elements into snippets to avoid duplication.
  • Group related prompts in the same set as multiple entries.

docs.title: Video Generation Guide
docs.text: Generate videos from text prompts or images using ziv-video or the Web UI.

docs.title: Supported Models
docs.text:
Alias Model Platforms I2V ltx-4 LTX-2.3, 4-bit: needs the least memory macOS, Windows, Linux ✅ ltx-8 LTX-2.3, 8-bit: closer to the full model, needs more memory macOS, Windows, Linux ✅

See Image Guide → Model Aliases for the full alias list.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
Use MODEL below as ltx-4 or ltx-8 (4-bit or 8-bit) on every platform.

# Text-to-video with LTX (4-bit)
ziv-video -m ltx-4 --prompt "A cat walking through a garden"

# Image-to-video with your platform alias
ziv-video -m MODEL --image photo.jpg --prompt "Camera slowly zooms in"

# Batch from prompts file with your platform alias
ziv-video -m MODEL -p prompts.yaml -r 3

# Square aspect, small size
ziv-video -m MODEL --ratio 1:1 --size s --prompt "Abstract art"

# A scene (who and where, look, camera) and what happens in it
ziv-video -m MODEL --scene "A knight in a grey castle courtyard, overcast, handheld camera." --prompt "She draws her sword and turns to the gate."

# Continue a clip with two more seconds (macOS)
ziv-video --extend clip.mp4 --prompt "She walks through the gate."

For image-to-video, the starting image is scaled to cover the video size with its shape kept, and whatever overflows is cropped from the center. Pick a --ratio close to the image's shape to keep all of it.

docs.title: Scene and Action
docs.text:
A video prompt holds two kinds of text, and the Web UI gives each its own box:

  • Scene is who and where, their look, the style and the camera setup. It describes the clip as a whole and stays the same from one clip to the next.
  • Action is what happens, in time order, with camera moves, sound and quoted dialogue. On the command line and in prompt files it is the prompt (--prompt, prompt:).

Both are optional, and you can ignore Scene and write everything in Action. Image workflows have no Scene.

The model receives the scene first, then the action. With no scene, it receives the action exactly as you wrote it. Text to Video and Image to Video need a scene or an action, and a scene alone is a valid run.

In the Web UI, Scene is the compact box above Action on the Text to Video, Image to Video and Extend Video workflows. The Your text and Enhanced tabs switch both boxes as a pair. From the command line, use --scene beside --prompt; in a prompt file, add scene: to an entry (see Prompts). A scene from --scene or the Workspace is the default for prompt-file entries that have none of their own.

The prompt enhancer works on the pair. One call returns a scene and an action:

  • Text to Video splits and expands what you wrote. Writing everything in Action is fine: the enhancer moves the setting, look and camera setup into the scene and the events into the action.
  • Image to Video keeps your scene as it is and writes only the action by default, the way Extend Video does: put what the image shows in Scene and what happens in Action. Use as reference on a gallery image fills Scene with the image's prompt and leaves Action empty for you. With a blank Scene, or with Scene and action chosen, it writes a short scene (style, and what the image does not show) and an action that describes the change.
  • Extend Video keeps the clip's scene as it is and writes only the action by default. See Extend a Video.

The Rewrite option chooses what is written: Scene and action, or Action only, which keeps your scene exactly as written and writes an action that fits it. It works in all three workflows (--enhance parts=action in ziv-video) and needs a scene: with none, both parts are written. See Rewrite. In the Web UI each part is used on its own: Generate sends a part's Enhanced text when it has any and your text otherwise, and Use mine next to a part goes back to your text for that part.

Reuse settings on a video fills both boxes. When the video was enhanced, Your text gets the text you typed and the Enhanced tab gets the rewrite of each part that was rewritten. A video made with Action only reuses with your scene and only the enhanced action.

docs.title: Prompt Enhancement
docs.text: Video prompts can be rewritten by the local prompt enhancer, which writes a scene and an action (see Scene and Action), adds visible motion and camera movement in time order and fits the action to the clip length. With audio on, the Sound options add ambience, sound effects, dialogue or music, and sounds you wrote are always kept. Use --enhance style=cinematic,motion=action+camera-move,sound=ambient+effects, or the Enhance options in the Web UI. For image-to-video, the rewrite describes motion and change rather than appearance; the enhancer does not see the starting image itself. Prompts are rewritten before the video model loads, and the enhancer is unloaded first, so it adds no memory during generation. In the Web UI, Cancel (or Esc twice) stops a video job while prompts are rewritten and at the next denoising step, in both passes of an upscaled video; while the model loads, and during the short latent upsample between the two passes of a Windows/Linux upscale, it takes effect once that finishes. Pause, Skip and Repeat are not available for video.

docs.title: Video Upscale & Audio
docs.text:
# Generate upscaled video (2x resolution)
ziv-video -m MODEL --upscale 2 --prompt "..."

# Upscaled video with custom step count
ziv-video -m MODEL --upscale 2 --steps 6 --prompt "..."

# Upscaled image-to-video
ziv-video -m MODEL --upscale 2 --image photo.jpg --prompt "Camera slowly zooms in"

# Strip audio from output
ziv-video -m MODEL --no-audio --prompt "..."

# Upscale + no audio
ziv-video -m MODEL --upscale 2 --no-audio --prompt "..."

--upscale 2 is the only supported video upscale mode. It works in two stages on every platform: the clip is rendered at half the requested width and height, its latents are upsampled 2× with the LTX-2.3 spatial upsampler, and a short refinement at full size sharpens the result. The finished clip has the width and height you asked for, and progress counts both stages as one run.

  • Steps — --steps (default 8, at most 8) sets the half-size stage. On Windows and Linux the refinement adds 3 steps, so the default run shows 11 steps in total. LoRAs apply to both stages.
  • Windows and Linux — the first upscale run downloads the upsampler (about 1 GB).
  • Size — width and height must be divisible by 64, and are aligned to 64 with a warning when needed.

Audio is generated together with the video on every platform, and --no-audio (or turning off Audio in the Web UI) removes it. On Windows and Linux the audio track is 48 kHz stereo AAC.

Windows and Linux video generation require CUDA. CPU fallback is not available for the diffusers video backend.

Each video records the settings it was made with, as images do (see Output Files); Reuse settings in the Web UI loads them.

docs.title: Review before upscaling
docs.text: --review works as for images (see Review before upscaling) on macOS, Windows and Linux. The small render is decoded to a short preview, so the pause adds a few seconds before the full-size pass. The sound may change slightly after upscaling.

docs.title: Video LoRA
docs.text:
# Single LoRA
ziv-video -m MODEL --prompt "A sunset" --lora /path/to/style.safetensors

# LoRA with custom weight
ziv-video -m MODEL --prompt "A sunset" --lora /path/to/style.safetensors:0.8

# Multiple LoRAs
ziv-video -m MODEL --prompt "A dance" --lora style.safetensors:0.5,motion.safetensors:0.8

macOS keeps the existing MLX LoRA behavior. Windows and Linux accept LoRAs only when the selected asset and installed diffusers runtime support the LTX adapter APIs in a diffusers-compatible format. Unsupported adapter APIs, unsupported file formats, and unsupported explicit scales fail before generation with a descriptive error.

docs.title: Extend a Video
docs.text: Extend continues a clip from where it ends: it generates what happens next, with audio, and writes a new file. Your original clip is never changed.

docs.title: Starting an extension
docs.text:
In the Web UI, start from any video in one of these ways:

  • Extend in the asset viewer or in the ⋯ menu of a video tile. In the viewer, press E.
  • The Extend Video tab, then Browse (or type a path) to choose a video on the machine running the server.
  • Reuse settings on a video that was itself an extension, which comes back with its source, scene, prompt and length.

The Workspace opens on Extend Video with the source shown under Source video, with its size, frame rate, length and whether it has audio. From the command line:

# Two more seconds (the default)
ziv-video --extend clip.mp4 --prompt "The camera pans to the tower."

# Four more seconds, at the source's frame rate
ziv-video --extend clip.mp4 --extend-seconds 4 --prompt "The camera pans to the tower."

# A frame count instead (rounded to a multiple of 8)
ziv-video --extend clip.mp4 --extend-frames 96

The result is written to the output folder like any video, with the settings it was made from embedded, including the source and the number of frames added. The extension takes the size and frame rate of the source. It also starts from the source's model and LoRAs when they are still available; choose others with -m and --lora.

docs.title: What can be extended
docs.text:
The video is checked before the model loads, and every problem is listed. A video can be extended when it:

  • has a video stream of at least 25 frames (about one second);
  • has a width and height that are multiples of 32 and at least 64 pixels each, as shown (the size after any rotation);
  • has a constant frame rate, square pixels, 8 bits per colour and no HDR;
  • is progressive, not interlaced;
  • was not upscaled (extend the original instead);
  • has audio that can be read at its end, if it has audio.

Clips made by the app pass. Clips from other tools pass when they meet the same rules. Phone clips that are stored sideways and rotated by a flag are supported: they are read and extended upright.

docs.title: Length
docs.text:
You set the length in seconds, at the source's frame rate, in steps of 8 frames. In the Web UI, Extend by (s) shows the frames it comes to (+48 frames) and Total shows the length of the whole result. At 24 fps, 2 s is 48 frames; at 30 fps it snaps to 64 frames (2.13 s). The default is 2 s and the minimum is 8 frames. There is no upper limit, but memory use grows with the length. The memory note under the length shows Tight or Too large when the extension may not fit; it never blocks Generate.

On the command line, --extend-seconds takes seconds and --extend-frames takes frames, rounded to a multiple of 8. A rounded value is reported when the job starts.

docs.title: Scene and action when extending
docs.text:
• Scene is kept from the source and editable. Its box is filled when you choose the source. The enhancer's Rewrite option is Action only by default when the clip has a scene, so it does not rewrite the scene and a chain of extensions keeps the same look. Choose Scene and action to rewrite the scene too. If you change the scene, Use the clip's scene puts the recorded one back.
  • Action starts empty with the hint "What happens next…". Write only the action that follows. An empty action continues naturally. With the enhancer on, it writes the action from your words, using the previous clip's action as context and without repeating its actions or its spoken lines.
  • Older clips, made before the Scene field existed, recorded one prompt only. Choosing one pre-fills Action with the old prompt and leaves Scene empty, so Rewrite uses Scene and action (Action only needs a scene). While Action still equals the old prompt, a warning says "Still the original prompt. Change it to what happens next." and Use the clip's prompt brings the old prompt back. Generate stays available. If you keep the old prompt anyway, the enhancer extracts a scene from it, and without the enhancer the quoted lines are dropped from the old prompt so its dialogue is not spoken again. Move the scene description into Scene to get the most from the extension.
  • Clips with no recorded prompt start with both boxes empty.

With the enhancer off, the scene is sent followed by the action. With ziv-video --extend, the scene defaults to the source's recorded scene and --scene replaces it.

docs.title: Audio
docs.text: Audio continues across the join. The new sound is generated from the end of the source's own sound, and the join is smoothed, so voices and ambience carry on. A silent source stays silent: the extension has no audio track. --no-audio (or turning Audio off in the Web UI) leaves the whole result without sound.

docs.title: The original part
docs.text: The original video is kept untouched when the new part can be attached to it as it is. Clips that the app made are joined this way, so the first part is identical to the source. Rotated clips, and clips from other tools that were encoded differently, are re-encoded once at high quality when joined: a small, one-time loss.

docs.title: Chaining and batches
docs.text: Extend a result to make the clip longer still: the extension is a normal video with the same scene, so it can be extended again. Several runs (-r) or several prompts make separate extensions of the same source. Each follows the usual seed rules; the source's seed is not reused.

docs.title: Memory
docs.text: The extension generates the last second of the source again (the part carried over) plus the new frames, so it needs the memory of a clip that long at the source's size, not of the whole result. Longer sources do not cost more.

docs.title: Known limits
docs.text:
• A faint change at the join. On very still shots, one frame at the join can look slightly different. It comes from the model's video encoder, which re-draws the carried second, and it is not smoothed over.
  • Fading audio in long chains. The model's sound can fade or thin out over many extensions of the same clip.

docs.title: Video Sizes
docs.text:
Default ratio is 16:9 and default size is s. Dimensions vary by --ratio.

Preset 16:9 9:16 1:1 xs 576×320 (49f) 320×576 (49f) 384×384 (49f) s 768×448 (49f) 448×768 (49f) 576×576 (49f) m 1024×576 (49f) 576×1024 (49f) 768×768 (49f) l 1280×704 (33f) 704×1280 (33f) 960×960 (33f) xl 1600×896 (25f) 896×1600 (25f) 1216×1216 (25f)

Every size is a multiple of 64, so --upscale 2 keeps it exact. xs is for quick prompt tests; m and l are 576p and 720p.

Use -W / -H to override with exact pixel dimensions.

docs.title: LTX Constraints
docs.text:
LTX-2.3 has specific alignment requirements that are auto-corrected with a warning:

  • Resolution: width and height must be divisible by 32 (64 when using --upscale)
  • Frames: must follow 8k+1 pattern (9, 17, 25, 33, 41, 49, ..., 97, 121). In the Web UI you set Duration (s) instead: it snaps to the nearest valid frame count at the model's frame rate (5 s at 24 fps is 121 frames), shows that count next to it, and has no upper limit. Longer clips need more memory (see Memory Check)
  • macOS MLX Q4 baseline: ltx-4, 704×448, ≤49 frames with --low-memory
  • macOS low memory: --low-memory (the default) frees each model component once it has run. On Macs with 24 GB of memory or less it also streams the transformer from disk during generation, which cuts the memory held while denoising; steps are slightly slower, and about twice as slow with a LoRA. --no-low-memory (or Low memory off in the Web UI) turns off both, keeping every component loaded

On Windows and Linux:

  • Memory — ltx-4 needs about 20 GB of system memory and ltx-8 about 27 GB; on a 32 GB machine use ltx-4. A model that cannot fit stops with an error before it loads. On a 32 GB machine each new prompt takes a little longer than repeating one (-r, or several seeds).
  • Length — on a 10 GB GPU with ltx-4, clips up to 20 s at M, 15 s at L and 10 s at XL fit, with or without --upscale 2.
  • First run — the first run of each model downloads it and prepares it for your GPU, which takes a while. Later runs start much faster.
  • Steps — at most 8 (--steps).

docs.title: Memory Check
docs.text:
Text to Video and Image to Video check the clip's size and length against the machine's memory before generating, and Extend Video checks the extension the same way (see Memory). On macOS the check is against the Mac's memory. On Windows and Linux it is against the GPU's memory and the system memory, once the model's files are downloaded. The check never blocks a job; it warns when the clip may run slowly or fail.

  • Web UI: under Duration (s), a note appears when the clip is tight (the Mac may slow down while generating; on Windows and Linux the GPU is nearly full or system memory is short) or too large (expect heavy swapping or an out-of-memory error). The note names the memory it is about. It follows the model, size, duration, Low memory and Upscale, and stays hidden while the clip fits. The memory badge on a video model is the estimate for a 5 s clip at 768×448 without upscale.
  • Command line: ziv-video prints one warning at the start of a run and carries on. Shorten the clip with --frames, use a smaller --size, and keep --low-memory on.

The estimate grows with the number of frames and the pixels per frame. On macOS it was measured with ltx-4 on a Mac with 32 GB of memory, for clips up to about 10 s at 704×448; far beyond that it is extrapolated. Macs with 24 GB or less stream the transformer from disk, so the estimate is on the high side there. On Windows and Linux it was measured on one 10 GB GPU with 32 GB of system memory, at ltx-4 and ltx-8: the GPU need stays flat for short clips and grows once a clip passes about 26,000 tokens at ltx-4 (for example 1408×896 beyond about 10 s), and it adds room for the allocator. On a card with more or less memory the thresholds are an extrapolation. It does not count memory already used by other apps or by an image model that is still loaded.

docs.title: Model Detection
docs.text:
ziv-video auto-detects the model family from supported model values:

  • Aliases — ltx-4 and ltx-8
  • Supported repo IDs — known LTX prefixes such as dgrauet/ltx* and Lightricks/LTX-Video*
  • Local paths — local paths containing ltx are treated as LTX candidates, including Windows-style path strings on any host

Arbitrary HuggingFace repositories are not accepted solely because their names contain ltx.

Runtime --lora values must be local LoRA files or bare LoRA names that resolve from ~/.ziv/loras/. HuggingFace-shaped LoRA references such as org/lora:0.8 are import inputs for ziv-model lora --hf, not direct generation inputs.

docs.title: Common Platform Errors
docs.text:
• LTX at q8 needs about 27 GB of system memory; this machine has 16 GB. Use ltx-4 instead. (Windows/Linux): pick the level the message names; ltx-4 needs the least memory.
  • LTX on Windows/Linux runs 4-bit or 8-bit...: the diffusers backend only loads LTX at a quantize level; use ltx-4 or ltx-8 instead of the repository ID.
  • CUDA is not available...: the diffusers video backend requires an NVIDIA CUDA device on Windows and Linux. When the message says to update the driver, install NVIDIA driver 580 or newer.
  • Could not detect video model family...: use an alias (ltx-4 or ltx-8), a known/configured LTX repo ID, or a local path containing ltx.

docs.text: • See Prompts Guide for prompt syntax, variables, structured prompts, and snippets.

docs.title: Entry Points
docs.text: Command Description ziv Unified parent command with subcommands: image, video, model, ui ziv-ui Standalone Web UI launcher ziv-image Image generation (standalone entry point) ziv-video Video generation (standalone entry point) ziv-model Model/LoRA management (standalone entry point)

docs.title: ziv — Unified Command
docs.text:
ziv is the parent command that dispatches to subcommands:

ziv image [options]    # Same as ziv-image
ziv video [options]    # Same as ziv-video
ziv model [options]    # Same as ziv-model
ziv ui [options]       # Same as ziv-ui

Running ziv with no subcommand prints command-discovery help and exits without starting a server. Use ziv ui or ziv-ui when you want to launch the Web UI.

Run ziv --help for available subcommands, or ziv <command> --help for command-specific options.

docs.title: ziv ui / ziv-ui — Web UI Launcher
docs.text:
The base package install includes the Web UI runtime, so ziv ui and ziv-ui work after a normal uv tool install z-vision-generator or uv sync. If a local environment is missing required Web UI packages, the launcher exits with repair guidance for the base install instead of pointing users at a second install step.

Argument Default Description --host 127.0.0.1 Host interface to bind the local Web UI server to. local is short for 0.0.0.0, which makes the UI reachable from other devices on your network; the launcher then also prints this machine's network address --port 8080 Preferred local port; the app chooses the next available port if this one is busy --no-browser off Start the server without opening a browser tab --background off Start the server in the background and return to the prompt once it is reachable. It keeps running after the terminal closes; its output goes only to the error log --background-stop off Stop every running Web UI server, whether started with --background or running in another terminal. Any job they are running stops too. Cannot be combined with --background

Every running server records itself in ~/.ziv/run/ (or $ZIV_DATA_DIR/run/), which is how --background-stop finds them. A server is asked to shut down first and is force-stopped if it has not exited after 10 seconds, together with any process it started. On Windows a server is stopped immediately. Servers started by versions before this flag existed are not recorded and must be stopped by hand.

The server only answers requests addressed to an IP address, localhost, the --host value, or (when bound to 0.0.0.0, :: or a LAN IP) this machine's hostname in both bare and .local form, and rejects state-changing requests from other sites. This protects against DNS-rebinding and cross-site attacks from pages open in the same browser. To reach the UI through another hostname, list it in ZIV_UI_ALLOWED_HOSTS (comma-separated), for example ZIV_UI_ALLOWED_HOSTS=studio.lan ziv-ui --host 0.0.0.0.

docs.title: --enhance spec
docs.text:
Comma-separated key=value pairs; join several values with +. Omitted keys use their defaults.

Key Values Default style keep, photo, candid, street, film, bw, portrait, product, cinematic, illustration, anime, comic, 3d, painterly keep mood keep, serene, joyful, romantic, melancholic, mysterious, eerie, dramatic, epic, whimsical, nostalgic keep details lighting, composition, camera, materials, color, environment, subject lighting+composition length shorter, same, longer, extra same motion (ziv-video only) action, camera-move, pacing action sound (ziv-video only, used with audio on) ambient, effects, dialogue, music none parts (ziv-video only) both, action action with --extend when the source has a scene, otherwise both

See Enhancing Prompts.

The ideo alias selects Ideogram 4 (ideogram-ai/ideogram-4-fp8), an image model on macOS (MLX), Windows and Linux (CUDA, using unsloth/ideogram-4-nf4-diffusers). Its width and height must be in the 256–2048 range and multiples of 16. Size presets that exceed this range — --size xl with --ratio 16:9 or --ratio 9:16 (2176 px) — are rejected before the model loads, as are --image and --upscale (both require img2img, which Ideogram 4 does not support).

Operational notes:

  • Video generation requires ffmpeg on every platform. If it is missing, ziv-video offers to install it with Homebrew or MacPorts (macOS), winget (Windows), or apt, dnf or pacman (Linux), and asks before running anything. On Windows, open a new terminal afterwards so PATH picks it up. On Fedora, dnf install ffmpeg needs RPM Fusion enabled.
  • Windows and Linux video generation are CUDA-only.
  • On Windows and Linux a model that cannot fit in system memory stops before loading, and the first run of each model takes a while to download and prepare it.

docs.title: Extending a video
docs.text:
ziv-video --extend clip.mp4 --prompt "The camera pans to the tower."
ziv-video --extend clip.mp4 --extend-seconds 4 --scene "A knight in a grey courtyard."
ziv-video --extend clip.mp4 --extend-frames 96 -p prompts.yaml

--extend checks the source before the model loads and refuses a video it cannot continue, naming every problem (see What can be extended). The output is a new file with the source's size and frame rate, and the original part is kept untouched when it can be stream-copied.

Defaults taken from the source when you do not pass them:

  • Scene: its recorded scene. --scene replaces it.
  • Model: the model it was made with, when that model is available locally; otherwise the configured default video model, with a warning.
  • LoRAs: the LoRAs it was made with that still exist; missing ones are skipped with a warning. --lora replaces them.
  • Prompt: none, so the extension continues naturally. A video recorded with a single prompt and no scene (made before scenes existed) keeps that prompt when you pass none, with quoted lines dropped while it is unchanged; if --prompt still equals it, a warning says to change it to what happens next.

Options refused with --extend, since the extension keeps the source's size and takes its own length: --image, --upscale, --ratio, --size, --width, --height and --frames. --extend-seconds and --extend-frames need --extend. In a prompt file, every entry needs a prompt, which is the action that follows the source. --no-audio leaves the result without sound, and a silent source gives a silent result. When the extension may not fit in memory, a warning is printed and the run continues.
